comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
Why only share the shuffle? Presumably smallquery has would also need to do distributed maps for certain queries?

Given the constraints of our infrastructure, it's not clear to me there's a huge difference between Zephyr and smallquery if you were creating them from first principles--they are both distributed data processing layers. They are making different design decisions (e.g. sql vs. Python), and sql certainly feels like the right choice for ad-hoc querying, but there's no reason it couldn't also handle the things written in Python / Zephyr today. The main infrastructure difference appears to be wanting smallquery to have hot workers so the queries are a little more interactive, which makes total sense to me, but still doesn't mean you couldn't use the same distributed sql engine with scheduling similar to Zephyr's today for the larger data processing jobs.

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
So before I propose this, it's worth calling out that I've had my head in Polars <> Zephyr for a while now and I'm worried everything might look like a Polars nail 😅.

That said, a somewhat crazy option to have a Rust / Python shuffle engine (which would work for sql via DataFusion) would be to use the [Zephyr Polars shuffle](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5963) and push the shuffle down into Polars via [map_groups](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/dataframe/api/polars.dataframe.group_by.GroupBy.map_groups.html#polars.dataframe.group_by.GroupBy.map_groups). We probably want to add a version of that function that takes a Rust UDF, to avoid the Python object overhead of the Python DataFrame object. At least in theory they are all using Arrow under the hood, so the conversion from DataFrame to whatever DataFusion wants should be zero-copy.

I'll work on a more coherent / detailed design proposal.

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
Worth noting the [limitations of distributed-datafusion](https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/index.html#when-not-to-use-this-library), specifically:
> * If any node fails mid-query, the whole query fails; there are no retries.
> * There’s no persistence of intermediate results, so queries can’t checkpoint or resume from where they stopped.

This is probably fine for the interactive workload, but this is the trap that our preemptable infra sets and it would be worth analyzing query runtime vs. node preemption to see what percentage of queries would fail and at what scale it becomes unusable.

comments.author: alxmrs
comments.body:
Here are my thoughts and impressions about which technology choices to make for the smallquery project: 

## DuckDB vs Polars vs DataFusion

These are all very similar but I think there are some important  differences that will lead us to decide that DataFusion is the right RDBMS engine to build atop of. 

Here is DataFusion's explanation of the differences between each project: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/faq.html#how-does-datafusion-compare-with-xyz

- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are very similar in goal (in process/embeddable OLAP query engine). DuckDB is built around its own internal format whereas DataFusion is designed to be agnostic of the core DB format. 
- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are modular and extensible, but DataFusion is the natural ancestor to Apache Arrow; see this post on [Composable Data Systems](https://wesmckinney.com/blog/looking-back-15-years/)
- DuckDB vs (DataFusion & Polars): C++ (sometimes, with Rust Extensions) vs a pure-rust ecosystem -- my preference is to go with Rust.
- Polars vs the rest: Polars is built on arrow, but is not designed as a "deconstructed database" like DuckDB and DataFusion, so it will be harder to integrate with. 

## Distribution 

Assuming DataFusion is the bet we go with, the next open question is Comet vs Ballista vs DataFusion Distributed: 

- Comet is DataFusion/Arrow within Spark, so I see this as really saying we should go with (better) Spark. While this is faster than Spark, it is still the slowest option in the distributed DataFusion ecosystem. This is lowest on my list, primarily because it adds a lot of system complexity (I count ~4-5 layers of abstraction between Zephyr, Spark, Comet, DataFusion, and Iris). The benefit, however, is that Comet happened to be a more popular choice than Ballista, even though I think Ballista is a better system. I think this might have to do with the amount of buy-in/popularity of Apache Spark.
- Ballista is the most mature way of distributing DataFusion. However, the DataFusion-Python to Ballista Python integration is somewhat far behind the primary version of DataFusion, making it suspect for us to want to depend on. (Warning: I could be wrong about this impression -- this is from recently trying to build on top of Ballista with Python a few months ago).
- DataFusion-Distributed is the new distributed system for DataFusion, and its core promise is to be a natural extension of the DataFusion data model (logical and physical plans). https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/. I like this choice for Iris because it delegates full control over how plans are distributed over workers, so I think it would give us more power to handle retries and preemption in an iris layer rather than the DB layer. It also should delegate to Iris actors with a more lightweight interface than Ballista. I also like that it looks like this system will be integrated into DataFusion-Python soon: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-python/issues/1612. That said, the concerns that Will pointed out from the "when not to use this section" may be dealbreakers, and the right bet is to integrate Ballista into Iris workers. 

I also just posted in the DataFusion Discord to ask what the maintainers recommend. It might be that the best way to find out would be to build a small prototype with DataFusion.

## Responses to the above discussion

>  still doesn't mean you couldn't use the same distributed sql engine with scheduling similar to Zephyr's today for the larger data processing jobs.
> Why only share the shuffle? Presumably smallquery has would also need to do distributed maps for certain queries?
> there's no reason it couldn't also handle the things written in Python / Zephyr today.

I am 100% on this team; I think a SQL engine is the core thing you need for doing ELT/ETL, even for [non-tabular data](https://github.com/jayendra13/zarr-datafusion).

> How much of this could we reuse from Datafusion/Ballista? It looks like the main gap there would be the shuffles do temp writes to local disk. We could bring some of those ideas in though.

I agree, I think reusing DB technology is better than reinventing it, especially since distributed shuffles for reductions are non-trivial. I think DataFusion-Distributed would fit in the cleanest with Iris, if we can handle retry logic and persistence (maybe that makes Ballista the winner -- my original intention with https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5861 was to have the DataFusion Context be swappable with a Ballista Context running on other workers in Iris). 

> ~100 sources, ~100k parquet files, ~35TB. In most cases we can assume parquet, but other formats would be nice to have.

35 TB is small. If we're looking for Marin Infra to support workloads in scientific applications like Coral, then we'd want to make sure this system scales to the 1s to 10s of petabytes IMO. We don't need to do this now, but it would be nice to know that such a thing is possible. (I still dream of loading all 12 PiBs of [ARCO-ERA5](https://github.com/google-research/arco-era5) into Marin). [Samudra](https://github.com/m2lines/Samudra), my primary project, is still looking for a core data engineering system replacement to Dask, and a 3 PiB dataset is on our roadmap to process.

> at some point I was curious if I could replace that with Arrow/Parquet, do you happen to have experience with that use-case? Scale ~20T. Actually, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4445 would be a good place to have this chat to keep this issue focused.

I'm part of the cult of [zarr.dev](https://zarr.dev), so I think Tensorstore on Zarr or maybe IceChunk is a better fit than parquet for Array shaped data. I think there could be a good opportunity to make a patch or extension to Orbax.

> I think it would probably look more like building sql support into Zephyr
> I'll work on a more coherent / detailed design proposal.

That's the dream. LMK if I can chat with you or collaborate on the design. I've done some work in this space.

comments.author: wmoss
claude[bot]
comments.body:
**Claude finished @wmoss's task in 2m 24s** —— [View job](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/28962455679)

---
### Ballista on Iris — deployment shape & failure model

I dug into how Zephyr deploys on Iris (the pattern you'd copy) and mapped Ballista's components onto it. TL;DR: deploying Ballista on Iris is mechanically easy and looks almost exactly like Zephyr's coordinator+workers; the hard part is exactly the one you flagged — **Ballista shuffles to executor-local disk, so an executor dying after it produced shuffle output forces recompute, and that recompute cascades under preemption.** Details below. I'd love @gabotechs to correct anything I get wrong about current Ballista internals.

---

### 1. The deployment is the easy part — it mirrors Zephyr almost 1:1

Zephyr already does the "scheduler + N executors per query" thing you're describing. One query = one Iris **job** that hosts the coordinator actor in-process and spins up an executor **actor group** as a child:

- `_run_coordinator_job` hosts the coordinator via `client.host_actor(...)` — [`execution.py:1543`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1543)
- executors are a sized child actor group — `client.create_actor_group(ZephyrWorker, ..., count=actual_workers, resources=..., actor_config=ActorConfig(max_task_retries=10))` — [`execution.py:1571`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1571)
- children are cascade-terminated when the coordinator job exits, so no orphaned executors ([`execution.py:6-11`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L4))

The Ballista analog:

| Ballista | Iris mapping |
|---|---|
| `ballista-scheduler` | one long-lived process — either the coordinator job itself, or a co-hosted actor (like Zephyr's in-process coordinator). Put it on the **non-preemptible** coordinator node from the design sketch above. |
| `ballista-executor` × N | a `create_actor_group(count=N)` of executor actors on preemptible workers, each running the executor gRPC server and registering with the scheduler |
| scheduler↔executor gRPC + Arrow Flight shuffle fetch | actor RPC endpoints; executors need to reach each other's Flight ports (Iris already gives every task a routable endpoint) |
| scheduler state store (in-mem / sled / etcd) | see §3 — this is where preemption survival is decided |

So "deploy scheduler + N executors per query" is a thin wrapper: a coordinator entrypoint that boots the scheduler, launches an executor actor group, submits the SQL, and writes results out. Nothing about Iris blocks this.

### 2. Executor failure — what actually happens

This is the crux. Ballista breaks the physical plan into **query stages** at every shuffle boundary. A `ShuffleWriterExec` at the end of a stage writes its output partitions as Arrow IPC files to the **executor's local disk**; the next stage's `ShuffleReaderExec` pulls those partitions from the producing executor over Arrow Flight.

Two distinct failure cases:

1. **Executor dies while running a task** → the scheduler sees the task fail / the executor heartbeat lapse, and reschedules that task onto another executor. This is fine — recompute one task from durable source data. Iris bringing up a replacement (the `max_task_retries` behavior) lines up with this; the new executor re-registers with the scheduler, just like Zephyr workers re-register after reconstruction ([`execution.py:351`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L351)).

2. **Executor dies *after* it finished a stage, and a downstream stage still needs its shuffle output** → that shuffle data was on local disk and is now **gone**. A reader hits a *fetch failure*. Ballista's recovery here is Spark-style: mark the lost shuffle partitions, and **re-run the map task(s) that produced them** (potentially the whole producing stage). Because the ultimate inputs are parquet in object storage, this is *recoverable in principle* — but under continuous preemption it **cascades**: re-running a producing stage means its executors write new shuffle files… which can also be lost before they're consumed. Query wall-time balloons; at enough scale/preemption rate the success probability collapses exactly as you predicted.

So the answer to "if an executor fails and Iris brings up another one, what happens?": the *running task* recovers cleanly, but any *already-materialized shuffle output on the dead node is lost and must be recomputed*, and that recompute is where preemption bites.

This is precisely why the design comment upthread proposes an **object-store shuffle with a per-attempt `_SUCCESS` committer** instead: once a stage's shuffle output is committed to GCS/CoreWeave, losing the executor costs you *nothing* — the durable partitions are still there, and a replacement executor just reads them. That's the property Zephyr already has (shuffle chunks live in the chunk store / object storage, not local disk), and it's the single most important thing Ballista does **not** give you out of the box.

### 3. Scheduler failure — does the whole query die?

Depends on the scheduler's state backend:

- **In-memory state (default single-scheduler)**: scheduler death = all job/stage/task state lost = **the query dies and cannot resume**. Restarting gives you a blank scheduler. This is the mode most people run.
- **Persistent state backend (sled embedded, or etcd in older versions)**: job graph and task/stage status are persisted, so a restarted scheduler can in principle recover in-flight jobs. In practice this path has historically been the less-exercised one, and it still doesn't rescue the lost *local-disk shuffle data* from §2 — it only rescues the *control-plane* state.

For Marin this means: keep the scheduler on the **non-preemptible** coordinator node (it's tiny — one per query), so scheduler loss is not a normal event. Then all the "can we survive preemption" weight lands on the executors, and the executor story only works if shuffle is durable (§2). Note this is a strictly *better* position than [datafusion-distributed's documented stance](https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/index.html#when-not-to-use-this-library) ("any node fails → whole query fails; no retries; no intermediate persistence") — Ballista at least *has* task reschedule + shuffle-recompute, which is why @gabotechs is steering you to Ballista over datafusion-distributed for the preemption constraint.

### 4. Net assessment for the smallquery constraint

- **Deploying Ballista on Iris**: straightforward, copy the Zephyr coordinator/executor-group pattern.
- **Executor preemption**: survivable but *expensive* out-of-the-box because of local-disk shuffle → recompute cascade. The fix is durable (object-store) shuffle output — the same thing the design notes and @rjpower/@wmoss's "reusable shuffle lib" thread are circling.
- **Scheduler preemption**: pin the scheduler to the non-preemptible node; don't rely on Ballista HA state recovery for the common case.

Concretely, if you want to validate the failure math you asked for, the cheapest experiment is: run a single distributed join on Ballista-on-Iris, kill an executor **after** its shuffle-producing stage completes but **before** the consuming stage reads it, and measure (a) does it recover, (b) how much recompute it costs. That directly exercises the §2 case and tells you whether default Ballista is viable or whether the object-store-shuffle swap is mandatory before this is usable on preemptible capacity.

I kept this to analysis (no code changes) since the ask was to look into feasibility. Happy to prototype the coordinator/executor-group wrapper or the kill-an-executor test harness if you want to turn this into a spike.
 · branch `claude/issue-6761-20260708-1728`

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
Thanks @ravwojdyla, now I feel like I better understand what use cases we want to support.

@alxmrs I agree that DataFusion feels like the right solution here and I think Ballista is the only reasonable choice.

If we want to support long-running / large jobs, I think we need to use GCS for checkpointing stage output instead of local disk. Otherwise I think the intersection of long processing times, lots of workers and those workers getting preempted is going to kill job performance or worse, make it never finish.

I had Gemini do an analysis of having Ballista checkpoint to GCS (attached) and it was actually somewhat promising. The main things I was worried about was that Ballista would likely create a lot of small files from the shuffle, which it does out of the box, but it also supports a sort-based shuffle that writes one large file and has reducers seek into it (this is what Zephyr does). I'm less worried than Gemini about the cost of updating all the call sites to support object storage since I think AI's costing models are generally based on pre-AI costs. It also seems like something that we could, hopefully, commit back to Ballista, since I definitely don't want to be maintaining a long-running fork.

As a first PoC, my suggestion would actually be to use `gcsfuse` to mount a GCS bucket to the local filesystem. It will certainly be less performant than changing the Ballista code, but wouldn't actually require any code changes to Ballista to get something up and running just to see if it works. 

@alxmrs, I'm going to take over from Rav on the infra side here, but if you're stoked on this feel free to take a crack at it and I'm happy to collaborate. Otherwise I can point an AI at it and see how far it can get, but I've got plenty to keep me busy so you're welcome to run with it.

Maybe I'm missing something, but from what I can see, they didn't do anything with shuffle. comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
🤖 **Status update: Distributed DataFusion-Ballista PoC & Comparison on Iris**

We stood up a DataFusion-Ballista distributed scheduler and executor pool on-Iris and evaluated its performance against the standard Zephyr pipeline for the text normalization step. See the [draft PR #7588](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7588) and the [detailed subissue #7266 comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7266#issuecomment-5065971169) for more information.

| Metric | Zephyr Pipeline | Ballista Pipeline (Optimized) | Speedup / Reduction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Normalize Step Time** | **1h 20m 24s** (80.4 min) | **5m 33s** (5.5 min) | **14.4× faster** |
| **Overall Wall Time** | 1h 20m 47s | 5m 33s (non-concurrent mode) | **14.5× faster** |
| **GCS Scan / Read Count** | 1 pass (6 GB read) | 1 pass per query (288 GB total scanned) | ~48× increase (sequential planning) |
| **Output File Correctness** | 22 parquet shards | 22 parquet shards | Identical shard count & schemas |

---

### ⚠️ Critical Downsides & Limitations of Ballista

While the raw execution speed is a massive improvement, we identified severe developer and scalability limitations when compared to Zephyr:

1. **No Distributed Python UDFs**: Remote executors cannot deserialize and run Python objects. This meant we were *unable* to implement the existing Zephyr logic exactly; many things had to be changed to similar SQL patterns (e.g., native regexp/hash/string expressions). Expressing these complex transformations in SQL results in highly nested, verbose query strings that are difficult to read and make the control flow opaque.
2. **No native Gzip NdJson/CSV support (`json.gz`)**: Ballista remote executors cannot parse gzipped raw formats. This means we could not directly process existing Nemotron files without first decompressing or converting them.
3. **Query Planning & Scan Duplication (Sharding Overhead)**: Zephyr handles sharding in-memory in a single pass. Ballista requires planning and submitting $2 \times N_{shards}$ separate SQL queries concurrently. Because each query filters rows using a hash (e.g. `WHERE hash(id) % 22 = i`), executors must scan the raw dataset once per query. On a full-scale dataset (e.g., 4,136 shards), coordinating 8,272 queries would cause planning overhead and total scanned bytes to explode.

comments.body:
🤖 **Follow-up correction: Engine Per-Core Throughput & Concurrency Audit**

Following an audit of CPU time (`cpu_time_total`), the initial 14× wall-time difference was heavily confounded by worker count (Ballista ran on 80 workers while Zephyr auto-scaled to 5). 

Evaluating actual per-core compute throughput shows:
* **Zephyr (Python/PyArrow)**: **2.03 MB/s** per CPU core
* **Ballista (Rust/DataFusion)**: **11.07 MB/s** per CPU core

**Top-line correction**: On an apples-to-apples per-core basis, **Ballista's execution engine is ~5.5× faster than Zephyr**.

issues.author: wmoss

This skill should be able to:
- Look at input files to determine how many shards
- Use the stats from #5995 to figure out how many threads / the ideal memory allocation

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md and skill playbooks
- [x] Check actionability (depends on #5995, several design choices unstated)
- [x] Survey existing zephyr skills and config surface
- [x] Post research + clarifying questions; no PR (design-sized, dep-blocked)

# Research

Two reasons this isn't PR-ready:

1. **Hard dep on #5995.** Bullet 2 ("use the stats from #5995") needs the `zephyr.stage` finelog stream from #5995, which isn't built yet — the proposed approach was just posted there today with open questions. A skill written against stats that don't exist will codify a fake schema. The skew-detection bullet has the same problem at per-shard granularity (`zephyr.shard`), and #5995's current scope explicitly defers per-shard rows.
2. **No definition of done for the skill itself.** The bullets describe *inputs to a heuristic*, not the skill's output, entry point, or scope. Concretely: where does the skill apply its recommendation (config file diff? new job submission? PR comment? chat reply?), what knobs does it touch (`map_workers_per_actor`, `reduce_workers_per_actor`, Iris `--memory`, scatter buffer fractions?), is it pre-job (plan from inputs only) or post-mortem (analyze a finished run) or mid-flight (suggest restart params)?

What's available today vs. what the skill would need:

| Need | Today | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| Shard count from inputs | [`readers.py#L98`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py#L98) `InputFileSpec`; row/byte ranges already supported | None — can list/size files via gsutil/fsspec |
| Per-stage throughput | [`execution.py#L191-L241`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L191-L241) `_stage_throughput` (in-process only) | Needs #5995 to land for cross-run history |
| Per-shard skew signal | [`OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/OPS.md) "Straggler Detection" — manual via `list-tasks` memoryMb + `actor call get_counters` | No durable per-shard counter stream (#5995 defers `zephyr.shard`) |
| Memory/thread knobs | [`execution.py#L1356`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1356) `map_workers_per_actor` / `reduce_workers_per_actor`; Iris `--memory` on `job run` | None |

**Relevant code**
- [`readers.py#L98-L125`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py#L98-L125) — `InputFileSpec`, the natural shard unit
- [`execution.py#L1356-L1416`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1356-L1416) — worker-slot knobs the skill would tune
- [`shuffle.py#L138-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L138-L142) — scatter buffer is `memory / num_workers`, so memory and worker-count tune together
- [`OPS.md` — Straggler Detection / Data Skew](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/OPS.md) — already documents the manual procedure a skill would automate
- [`.agents/skills/babysit-zephyr/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/babysit-zephyr/SKILL.md) and [`evaluate-zephyr-perf/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/evaluate-zephyr-perf/SKILL.md) — style/scope precedents (this skill is the missing third leg: pre-flight planner / post-mortem optimizer)

# Proposed approach (needs sign-off before writing the skill)

Split into two skills along the pre-job / post-job seam, since they use disjoint inputs and produce disjoint outputs:

**A. `plan-zephyr` (pre-job, no #5995 dep).** Input: a submission script or pipeline plan. Skill:
1. Resolves `InputFileSpec`s, enumerates files via fsspec, captures size and (for parquet) row counts.
2. Reports shard count and shard-size distribution (p50/p95/max/skew-ratio).
3. Picks `map_workers_per_actor`, `reduce_workers_per_actor`, and Iris `--memory` from a small heuristic table (e.g. memory = max(scatter-buffer-floor, p95 shard bytes × buffer-multiple); workers = min(cpu_count, p95-shard-mem-fit)).
4. Emits a diff against the user's submission command + a one-paragraph rationale. Does **not** auto-submit.

Doable now. ~100 LOC of skill prose + a small `scripts/zephyr/plan_inputs.py` helper for file enumeration (the heuristic itself stays in the skill prose; agents apply judgment).

**B. `tune-zephyr` (post-mortem, blocked on #5995).** Input: a finished or in-flight `iris_job_id`. Skill:
1. Pulls `zephyr.stage` rows for the run; flags stages where `item_rate` collapsed late (straggler signature) or `peak_worker_memory_mb` was close to allocation (under-provisioned).
2. Cross-references `iris.worker` (already exists) for OOM/preemption.
3. For skew, falls back to manual `actor call get_counters` per OPS.md until #5995 ships `zephyr.shard`.
4. Emits a recommended config delta for the next run, plus a "re-shard the input" recommendation when input skew is the dominant cost.

Out-of-scope for now (flag if you disagree):
- Auto-resubmitting with new params — risky without human review.
- Modifying scatter internals (covered by `evaluate-zephyr-perf`).
- CPU sizing — Iris already sets that per cluster config; not a Zephyr-side knob.

**Questions for @wmoss before I write either skill:**

- **(a) Split A/B or single skill?** I lean two skills (different inputs, different cadences, B blocks on #5995). Push back if you want one entry point.
- **(b) Output channel.** Print to terminal in the invoking chat (like `debug`), comment on a PR (like `evaluate-zephyr-perf`), or write a recommended config file? My default: terminal for A, comment on the issue/PR that owns the run for B.
- **(c) Heuristic provenance.** Do you have an existing rule-of-thumb for memory-per-shard / workers-per-actor I should encode, or should I derive defaults from a few representative ferries (datakit tier1/tier2/tier3) and bake those numbers in?
- **(d) Skew action.** When the skill flags skewed input shards, what's the recommended remediation in this codebase — a `repartition`/`reshuffle` op, manual `InputFileSpec` row-range splits, or just "tell the user and stop"?
- **(e) Defer B until #5995 lands?** Or stub it now against the proposed schema and update when #5995 lands?

Holding off on PRs pending answers, since (b)–(d) materially change the skill's content.

issues.author: wmoss
issues.body:
Parent issue for tracking work to get to a stable (version 1?) of Zephyr. This issue should be the home for everything required for the tactical burn down of Zephyr, as outlined in [State of the Infra -- May 2026](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1tw-KevlFPRHQzXCDZeRfluPCk84QroJsn1zvHY8EzPE/edit?tab=t.0). The goal of this epic is also to provide a way to think bigger and longer term about Zephyr.

# Out of scope
Notably out of scope for this is providing a way to write sql to run distributed jobs over our infrastructure. We have discussed using [smallpond](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/smallpond) or attempting to push DuckDB deeper into Zephyr, but both of those are out of scope for this. Users will be able to use sql (using DataFusion or DuckDB) to process `RecordBatch` objects in mappers or reducers.

issues.author: ravwojdyla
issues.body:
Finelog in `cw-us-east-02a` stopped ingestion, publication, and forwarding at about 07:27 UTC on 2026-11-23. All 26 namespaces stopped advancing. RSS increased from 1.87 GiB to 22.1 GiB while the ingest buffer stayed at 78,458 bytes. The pod remained Ready with zero restarts. [Incident 1046](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/1046) contains the evidence and recovery constraints.

Same-pod inspection found all 512 blocking workers occupied:

- 510 workers wait on one registration mutex in `Store::register_table_with`.
- One worker holds that registration mutex and waits in `TableRuntime::update_policy`.
- One worker waits for the query-visibility write lock in `archive::evict_segment`.

Symbolic stacks from three representative threads confirm these call paths. The binary reports commit `20f92312db`, tree `6f0a1b5712`.

The [eviction call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20f92312db/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/maintenance.rs#L199) passes `&runtime.storage_policy.lock().unwrap().clone()` directly to `evict_to_policy`. Rust retains the temporary mutex guard until the call returns. Eviction therefore holds the policy mutex while it waits for query visibility. [Registration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20f92312db/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/store.rs#L1042) holds its registration mutex while `update_policy` waits for that policy mutex.

The [forwarding read](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20f92312db/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/forwarding.rs#L958) holds a visibility read guard while it awaits snapshot work in the same blocking pool. Its timeout applies after snapshot acquisition. This permits a deadlock when registration requests fill the pool. The specific async reader that owns the live lock was not directly inspected.

Reproduce the mutex defect (proposed deterministic regression case, not yet run):

1. Create a legacy table with an archived segment eligible for eviction.
2. Hold the process-wide visibility read lock and start eviction.
3. Wait until eviction requests the visibility write lock.
4. Attempt a policy update or re-registration before releasing the read lock.

Expected: The policy update completes while eviction waits.

A separate saturation test must confirm that registration waits cannot exhaust the workers that readers require to release visibility guards.

Release the policy mutex before the eviction call, with a separate `let policy = runtime.storage_policy.lock().unwrap().clone();` statement. Add the regression test above. Also bound the entire forwarding read, including snapshot acquisition, and control registration admission before it occupies blocking workers.

The operator approved a restart of only the Finelog container. Kubernetes restarted it at 08:30:10 UTC in the same pod, preserving the cache. Startup recovered an unpublished local log revision. By 08:32 UTC, ingestion, publication, and settled cursors advanced. A recent regional task-log timestamp also appeared in the hub. RSS fell from 24.9 GiB before restart to 0.60 GiB at 08:32:44 UTC.

No code fix is deployed, so the defect can recur. Recovery of all outage data remains unverified and depends on producer retention and retry. The incident record contains the recovery commands and evidence.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

On current `main` (`ec7d425185`), eviction retains the policy mutex through `evict_to_policy` while registration holds a table's registration mutex and waits in `update_policy`; concurrent registrations can occupy the blocking pool. The forwarder holds a visibility read guard while its snapshot waits in that pool, and its 60-second timeout is enforced only after snapshot acquisition. [Incident 1046](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/1046) records 510 registration waiters and two other blocked workers; no open PR covers this incident.

**Relevant code**
- [`maintenance.rs#L194-L210`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ec7d42518566ee77f058a9b9da34b0b2b41c79ce/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/maintenance.rs#L194-L210) — policy guard spans eviction.
- [`archive.rs#L211-L219`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ec7d42518566ee77f058a9b9da34b0b2b41c79ce/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/legacy/archive.rs#L211-L219) — eviction requests visibility write lock.
- [`store.rs#L1040-L1065`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ec7d42518566ee77f058a9b9da34b0b2b41c79ce/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/store.rs#L1040-L1065) — registration lock spans runtime update.
- [`forwarding.rs#L955-L967`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ec7d42518566ee77f058a9b9da34b0b2b41c79ce/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/forwarding.rs#L955-L967) — read guard spans blocking snapshot.
- [`stats_service.rs#L165-L195`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ec7d42518566ee77f058a9b9da34b0b2b41c79ce/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/stats_service.rs#L165-L195) — registration enters blocking pool.

# Proposed Fix

1. In `TableWork::Eviction`, clone `storage_policy` into a local variable before calling `evict_to_policy`, releasing its mutex before any visibility wait. Add a deterministic regression test with an eligible archived segment: hold a visibility read guard, start eviction, verify a policy-only re-registration completes while eviction waits, then release the guard and verify eviction finishes.
2. Enforce an outer forward-read timeout starting before visibility acquisition and covering the blocking snapshot; retain the scan deadline. Verify that a stalled snapshot times out, releases the read guard, and leaves the forwarding cursor unchanged.
3. Admit `RegisterTable` before `spawn_blocking` with a bounded permit pool. Move each permit into its blocking closure so client cancellation cannot free capacity while its worker still runs. Test with a constrained blocking pool and more simultaneous registrations than permits; a forwarding snapshot must still obtain a worker.
4. Run the Finelog Rust tests and repository lint/review gates, then open one PR with `Fixes #12024`. Check ingestion and forwarding progress after deployment; the incident's restart and cache-loss constraints still apply to any recovery action.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body: 🤖 The confirmed blocking chain starts at the [eviction call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20f92312db/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/maintenance.rs#L199). Its temporary policy guard stays locked while eviction waits for readers. I will release that guard before the call and add a regression that verifies a policy update can finish while eviction waits for visibility. This PR will repair the observed cause. Full forwarding deadlines and registration admission remain separate hardening work.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 The fix is complete in local branch `agent/20261123-fix-12024` at commit `a5c87f523d`.

Eviction now clones the storage policy in a separate statement, which releases the mutex before `evict_to_policy` waits for query readers. The regression test failed before the fix and passed after it. The full source checks passed: 690 Rust tests and 140 Python tests, with three Rust tests ignored. The macOS checks used a canonical temporary path and UTC. The same path and timezone failures occurred on the unchanged base branch.

Independent review and repository lint review completed. The supplied GitHub account cannot push to this repository or create a fork. Publication is pending access. The recovered pod remains Ready with one container restart, and publication and forwarding continue to advance.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The SkyRL CPU launcher can select a cached Python build without Linux pidfd support and fail before evaluation workers start.

Reproduce:
1. Run a Linux task whose image provides a compatible Python with `os.pidfd_open`, while the shared uv cache contains a compatible managed build without that API.
2. Use `skyrl_cpu_command` to construct a rollout worker in the frozen SkyRL CPU environment.
3. Observe that uv selects the managed build and Shellbox keeper allocation raises `AttributeError: module 'os' has no attribute 'pidfd_open'`.

Expected: nested SkyRL interpreter selection follows the task image's compatible system interpreter, and worker preflight verifies the required pidfd capability before allocating GPUs.

In the observed case, task setup selected image CPython 3.12.16, but the nested environment selected cached CPython 3.12.12. Both processes ran on Linux. `--no-python-downloads` prevents a download; it does not prevent selection of an existing managed build. Iris task setup already prefers the image interpreter, but the nested SkyRL launcher does not.

The branch fix is [1e1d04c3c2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1e1d04c3c2ebb9791ee2a224a5e839b34ae583d3). A real-uv regression fails against the unchanged launcher and passes with the fix. A Linux CPU qualification built the real rollout worker with the original evaluation document on image CPython 3.12.16.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`skyrl_cpu_command` lets both nested uv selections use a cached managed Python even when the task image has a compatible system Python. A managed build missing `os.pidfd_open` fails during Shellbox worker construction; `--no-python-downloads` does not exclude cached builds. The fix exists on [the long-loop prototype PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120), whose broader branch currently has merge conflicts.

**Relevant code**
- [`skyrl.py#L875-L905`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cddf4805ec/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L875-L905) — nested uv selections
- [`test_skyrl.py#L139-L216`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cddf4805ec/tests/rl/test_skyrl.py#L139-L216) — real-uv launcher regression

# Proposed Fix

`skyrl_cpu_command()` starts uv's tool runner, which starts the frozen SkyRL environment; either selection can choose the cached build. Apply `--python-preference system` at both selections, and extend the real-uv test to verify that the nested process uses the image interpreter despite a cached managed build. Extract this issue-sized fix from the prototype branch onto current `main`.

The real-uv regression failed before the change by selecting the cached managed build and passes with the image interpreter selected; all 89 local RL tests, full lint, branch review, and CI passed. CI's first run ended at pytest's 600-second session timeout after 358 tests passed; the rerun passed. The worker-construction preflight remains in the long-loop prototype PR #11120, where its experiment files live.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Slow final hooks can turn completed optimizer updates and a saved final checkpoint into a failed multi-host job.

Reproduce:
1. Initialize two JAX processes with `shutdown_timeout_seconds=2`.
2. Delay process 0 for 5 seconds after computation, while process 1 calls `jax.distributed.shutdown()`.
3. Both processes abort. The shutdown barrier reports 1/2 processes present and process 0 missing. This CPU reproduction was run locally; it does not exercise GPU kernels or object-store uploads.

Observed on a 32-process H100 SFT run at source `cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65` on 2026-11-22:
- Process 0 completed step 527 (528 updates) at 16:14:10UTC. Its native checkpoint committed at 16:15:27UTC; the HF export finished at 16:35UTC.
- Processes 1–31 logged completion of their final XLA-dump uploads at 16:39:33–43UTC. Process 0 has no corresponding upload-completion line.
- At16:41:33UTC, the shutdown barrier failed with 31/32 processes present. Process 27 entered first; process 0 was missing.
- Process 1's Python stack ends in `jax.distributed.shutdown()`, called by `_finalize_iris_jax_after_clean_exit`. Iris reports exit 139. The PyArrow/Torch names are the loaded-extension footer, not a causal stack.
- The task timeout was 72000 seconds. The failure occurred at the 120-second JAX shutdown deadline after the first process entered shutdown.
- The training completion receipt was not published. The exact operation delaying process 0 is not recoverable from the fatal signal-handler dump; final-hook/upload skew is supported by the logs, but an upload deadlock is not proven.

The relevant paths are [the Levanter exit handler](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/levanter/src/levanter/distributed.py#L36), [the forced final hooks](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L738), [the synchronous dump uploader](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/levanter/src/levanter/callbacks/profiler.py#L190), and [Iris's shutdown timeout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py#L48).

Expected: all processes finish required finalization before distributed shutdown starts. Publish the committed-checkpoint/control receipt before optional debug uploads. Bound those uploads and use a symmetric, bounded finalization rendezvous before shutdown. A delayed-process regression must preserve genuine training failures and must not relabel an unfinished checkpoint as complete.

Related closed incidents: #6907 and #7372 involved W&B teardown. This occurrence shows final-hook skew before the completion receipt; the process 0 blocker remains to be isolated.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body: 🤖 Incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/1042. The two-process CPU reproduction confirms that a late process can abort both processes at distributed shutdown; it does not establish the exact operation delaying production rank zero. The native completion receipt remains absent.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`Trainer.train()` forces final hooks, and `run_hooks()` calls the XLA dump uploader synchronously on every rank after those hooks. Rank 0 calls Iris `complete_job` only after its JAX shutdown; 31/32 ranks entering the shutdown barrier establishes skew, but the blocked operation on rank 0 remains unknown. Iris `complete_job` marks unfinished tasks successful and stops them, so moving it before uploads would create a false success path.

**Relevant code**
- [`trainer.py#L372-L375`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/18a6cd6463ddb867378628d1ac4beba07cf33312/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L372-L375) — synchronous dump upload after hooks
- [`trainer.py#L420-L445`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/18a6cd6463ddb867378628d1ac4beba07cf33312/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L420-L445) — final checkpoint commit wait
- [`profiler.py#L190-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/18a6cd6463ddb867378628d1ac4beba07cf33312/lib/levanter/src/levanter/callbacks/profiler.py#L190-L215) — unbounded per-file upload loop
- [`distributed.py#L36-L46`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/18a6cd6463ddb867378628d1ac4beba07cf33312/lib/levanter/src/levanter/distributed.py#L36-L46) — shutdown before job completion
- [`batches.py#L371-L399`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/18a6cd6463ddb867378628d1ac4beba07cf33312/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/batches.py#L371-L399) — completion stops unfinished tasks

# Proposed Fix

1. Log per-rank start and end of forced hooks, checkpoint wait, configured HF export, XLA upload, tracker finish, and JAX shutdown. Identify rank 0's delayed phase from a reproduction or retained logs before attributing this incident to an upload.
2. Split required finalization from optional diagnostics. Await the final native checkpoint commit and any required export before publishing a checkpoint-ready receipt with the completed step and checkpoint path. Keep Iris `complete_job` after coordinated shutdown.
3. Move the final XLA dump upload out of `run_hooks`; give the transfer a deadline that can stop blocked I/O, and record an upload timeout as a diagnostic failure. A thread wait alone cannot stop a blocked upload.
4. After each rank finishes required finalization and its bounded optional work, enter a named, bounded rendezvous before `jax.distributed.shutdown()`. A missing rank or failed required operation must fail the job and must not publish completion.
5. Add a real two-process CPU regression with rank 0 delayed beyond the JAX shutdown timeout, plus blocked-upload and failed-checkpoint cases. Verify successful runs publish one completion receipt, while required failures publish none; then validate the finalization sequence on a small H100 run with dump upload enabled.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Snapshot of realized step times, token volumes and GPU allocations for Mochi and Snowball RL and SFT, taken on 2026-11-23 from Finelog trainer markers, run logs and #8089. "Realized" is wall time per step including evaluation and buffer refill. RL tokens are learner-consumed response and loss tokens; SFT tokens are packed positions (batch × sequence length).

## RL

| Model / run | GPUs | Tokens per step | Typical step (no eval) | Realized average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mochi `.123` (96k response cap) | 128 GB200 (48 trainer + 80 rollout) | 32 prompts × 8 = 256 sequences; ~1.3–1.4M response, ~0.5–0.9M loss | ~175 s (optimizer ~125 s) | ~1,620 s over steps 2–11; evaluation every 3 steps plus refill |
| Mochi `.124` (priority eval drain) | 128 GB200 | as `.123` | — | full step 3: 1,142 s vs 2,254 s for `.123`; failed at step 4 on a drain bug, since fixed |
| Snowball Exp5 `.140` (long-loop round 5) | 256 H100 (80 trainer + 176 inference) | 64 prompts × 8 = 512 sequences; ~5.8–6.6M response, ~3.6–4.4M loss | ~165–850 s | ~1,940 s over steps 2–5; validation every 2 steps; optimizer CPU offload |
| Snowball resize, GB200 (65k context) | 64 GB200 | not recorded | 195 s/update | ≈ typical |
| Snowball resize, H100 | 112 H100 (80 trainer + 32 rollout) | not recorded | 170 s/update (42.5% rollout wait) | ≈ typical |
| Snowball `speed-medium` preset (#11975) | 40 H100 (32 learner + 8 inference) | ~2.1M response | 85 s plain, 56 s with DSpark | ≈ typical |

## SFT

| Model / run | GPUs | Tokens per step | Realized step | Throughput |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mochi SFT production run (#8089, 10.05 mix) | 11 GB200 NVL72 racks (~792 GPUs) | 176 × 262,144 ≈ 46.1M | 29.3 s median; 6,916 updates in 58.0 h | ~1.57M tok/s, ~2.0k tok/s/GPU |
| Mochi SFT run on cw-us-east-08a, 2026-11-23 | 128 GB200 | 32 × 262,144 ≈ 8.4M (from logged hyperparameters) | 9.3 s/it | ~0.90M tok/s, ~7.0k tok/s/GPU |
| Snowball Exp5 SFT (V7 mix) | 256 H100 | ≈ 67M, assuming 256 × 262,144 packing as in V9 (not read from this run's logs) | ~115 s/it trainer rate; ~124 s wall (475 steps in 16 h 25 min) | ~0.58M tok/s, ~2.3k tok/s/GPU |

## Observations

- RL realized time is about 10× the training step for both models. Evaluation and rollout-buffer refill dominate, not optimizer compute.
- Per step, Snowball Exp5 consumes about 4× Mochi's response tokens (512 vs 256 sequences, longer agentic histories) in similar realized time.
- Mochi SFT on 128 GB200 delivers about 3.5× the per-GPU token throughput of the 11-rack run.
- The cleanest Snowball RL throughput figures are 195 s/update on 64 GB200 and 170 s/update on 112 H100.

issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
issues.body:
Four generated Reasoning Gym tasks give full reward to a reply that does not depend on the question. `reasoning_gym_generated` holds 1,000 rows of each.

- `game_of_life_halting`: every non-blank reply scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer compares `bool(reply)` with `bool(answer)`, and every answer is the string `True` or `False`. [The generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/generate.py#L77-L86) records the reward of the fixed wrong answer `definitely wrong` for every row. For these 1,000 rows the recorded reward is 1.0, and [`convert_generated`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/tasks.py#L256-L271) stores the record without reading it.
- `complex_arithmetic`: the reply `NaN` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer returns `min(1.0, math.exp(-distance))`, which is 1.0 when the distance is NaN.
- `coin_flip`: the reply `0` scores 1.0 on 939 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 gives partial reward for a matching prefix and divides by the length of the shorter string, so the one-character reply `0` matches every answer that starts with `0.`.
- `propositional_logic`: the reply `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on 820 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer accepts any conclusion that follows from the premises, and a disjunction that names a premise follows from it.

Reproduce:

1. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONHASHSEED=0 uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra reasoning-gym python - <<'EOF'
   import sys

   sys.path.insert(0, "experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym")
   import generate
   import reasoning_gym

   replies = (
       ("game_of_life_halting", "x"),
       ("complex_arithmetic", "NaN"),
       ("coin_flip", "0"),
       ("propositional_logic", "P ∨ Q"),
   )
   for task, reply in replies:
       data = reasoning_gym.create_dataset(task, size=generate.ROWS_PER_TASK, seed=generate.task_seed(task))
       score = reasoning_gym.get_score_answer_fn(task)
       print(task, repr(reply), sum(score(reply, data[index]) == 1.0 for index in range(generate.ROWS_PER_TASK)))
   EOF
   ```

2. It prints `game_of_life_halting 'x' 1000`, `complex_arithmetic 'NaN' 1000`, `coin_flip '0' 939` and `propositional_logic 'P ∨ Q' 820`.

Expected: a constant reply does not earn full reward.

The recorded wrong answer scores 0 on `complex_arithmetic` and `coin_flip` and 0.05 or 0.25 on `propositional_logic`, so that record shows only the first of the four. Two of the four are in the Nemotron blend's part of the released validation panel (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Data`): with the panel's own grade script, `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on six of its seven `propositional_logic` tasks and `NaN` on its one `complex_arithmetic` task.

I tried 44 constant replies on the first 100 entries of every generated task. No fifth task gives the full reward on more than a quarter of the entries to a constant that is not the entry's answer.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 A fifth task belongs on this list: `puzzle24`. The reply `1*2*3*4` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 of its generated entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 (`reasoning_gym/games/puzzle24.py` L114-L132) checks that the reply evaluates to 24 and contains four numbers between 1 and 10. It does not read the entry's numbers. Five of the 1,000 entries have the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4. The recorded wrong answer `definitely wrong` scores 0.01 on every entry, so that record does not show it.

The last paragraph of the issue says that no fifth task pays a constant on more than a quarter of its entries. None of the 44 constants I tried evaluates to 24, so that sweep could not find this task.

To check, add `("puzzle24", "1*2*3*4")` to `replies` in the script above. It prints `puzzle24 '1*2*3*4' 1000`. `puzzle24` is not in the released validation panel.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 After #11987, `propositional_logic` still pays a reply that ignores the question, and it pays most correct conclusions 0. The task asks for "a correct conclusion", and the merged scorer compares the reply's text with the entry's `example_answer`, which is one of many valid conclusions. On the 1,000 generated entries (reasoning-gym 0.1.25, the generator's seeds), with the scorer on main `18a6cd646`:

- The 1,000 entries have 61 distinct examples. `(P ∨ Q)` is the example on 73 of them, so the constant reply `(P ∨ Q)` scores 1.0 on 73.
- Restating one of the entry's premises as the conclusion scores 1.0 for 81 of the 2,998 premises. The pinned scorer gave 1.0 to the 1,759 that are not trivial.
- Comparing with the example by truth table, as the review on #11987 suggested, would raise the constant `(P ∨ Q)` to 132 entries. 344 of the 2,998 premises are equivalent to their entry's example.

So comparing with the recorded example does not measure inference here, and the pinned scorer's rule (any entailed formula that is not trivial) admits the weakening `P ∨ Q`. I don't see a per-entry rule that rejects that weakening and still accepts the generator's own examples, because many examples are weakenings themselves: seed 42's first entry has the premises `R` and `Q` and the example `(P ∨ Q)`. Leaving the family out of training and the validation panel until the task asks for a specific conclusion looks cleanest to me. @penfever, would you rather keep the rows and accept that, or have me send a PR that excludes the family?

The coin_flip tolerance from the same review is in #12006.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** Long-loop rounds regressed from Exp1 (SFT 746 → RL 16: Micro scored-attempt mean 0.4526, mean of benchmark means 0.5216; SFT 746 alone 0.4023 / 0.4798) to Exp2 (SFT 204 → RL 20: 0.4048 / 0.4829) and Exp4 (SFT 360 → RL 36: 0.3763 / 0.4250; issue 11337), while several SFT settings (along with data and RL) changed at the same time. Isolating which SFT setting change(s) account for the drop directly informs the SFT recipe for Mochi.
- **Goal:** Identify which SFT setting change(s) between Exp1 and Exp4 account for lower general and agentic ability.
- **Data:** Fixed 10/05 SFT full-mixture catalog (216 SFT stores plus pretraining replay) starting from the pre-train Snowball base, held constant across every arm so data-release changes do not confound SFT recipe settings. The 8-hour bank-optimizer runs reported below use the 19 Nov / 6164 Snowball SFT mix (20.47% pretraining replay) from the same pre-train Snowball base.
- **Method:** SFT only, changing one verified Exp1-to-Exp4 setting at a time from the Exp1 baseline settings; run at one-hour scale first and then 8-hour scale for decisive arms, scoring every checkpoint on Micro210 and the edit-call eval. The 8-hour comparison changes one setting, the optimizer rule for the 4-D expert banks (Muon-H, Adam, or an RMSProp-style rule), and also scores held-out loss.
- **Results:**
  - **8-hour arm E r2 (expert banks on Adam) vs the 20.47% control (Muon-H on every matrix):** both on the 19 Nov / 6164 data and model, step 500, trainer seed 0, trained and scored on cw-rno2a, one run each. Held-out SFT loss is 0.4488 vs 0.5413. Edit-call rates are equal within their intervals (all 10 overlap; pooled applied edits 0.825 vs 0.765). Micro210 (14 clean sources, two repeats) is 57.70% vs 45.18% (+12.52 pp). Details: [held-out loss](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7078520306), [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7080258692), [Micro210](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7081822894).
  - **8-hour arm F (expert banks on an RMSProp-style rule, second moment only, no momentum):** same setup, but trained on a different code commit; its config differs from arm E r2 only in the bank rule. Held-out SFT loss is 0.4433. Sampled edit-call applied edits are 0.674, below arm E r2 (0.825) and the control (0.765), with non-overlapping intervals. Micro210 is 50.51%: 7.19 pp below arm E r2 and 5.33 pp above the control, but its two repeats do not separate clearly from the control's. Details: [arm F at 8 hours](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7087782018).
- **Conclusion:** At 8 hours, expert banks on Adam is the only bank rule that is clearly above the Muon-H control on Micro210. The one-array RMSProp-style rule reaches about the same held-out SFT loss (0.4433 vs 0.4488) but not the same capability scores, and it trained on a different code commit. One training run per arm; no cause is claimed.

Parent: issue 11535. Related: issue 11337 (Snowball recipe scoreboard) and issue 11793 (first-update hang when running Exp1's optimizer assignment with FP32 stored weights on the current long-loop runtime).

## Verified Exp1–Exp4 SFT settings

Every setting below comes from direct source inspection at each run's commit (Exp2 from its archived consumed config):

| Setting | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`) | Exp3 (`0f5721bbb4`) | Exp4 (`09ac3d5afd`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Optimizer | `grug_moe_muonh_v1` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py`) | Plain Adam on all parameters | `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py`) | Same as Exp3 |
| 4-D routed expert banks | Adam (`adam_lr`) | Adam | Muon-H | Muon-H |
| Norm scales | Muon-H (stacked 2-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `lm_head` / `output_proj` | AdamH (main LR) | Adam | AdamH (main LR) | Same as Exp3 |
| Peak LR | `5e-5` (both groups) | `5e-5` | Muon-H/AdamH `5e-5`; Adam group `1.1538e-5` (`5e-5 × 3/13`) | Same as Exp3 |
| Betas / eps | Optimizer defaults (`0.9 / 0.95 / 1e-8`) | `0.9 / 0.95 / 1e-8` | `0.9062 / 0.95 / 3.83e-15` | Same as Exp3 |
| LR schedule | Linear, decay 475, horizon 4,750, min `0.1×`; stopped at 746 → **constant `5e-5`** | Cosine over all 204 updates to `0.1×` | Linear, decay 475, horizon 4,750; ran 388 of 746 → **constant** | **Linear over all 360 updates to `0.1×`** (both groups) |
| Weight decay | `0` | `0` | `0.1` passed, **inert** (not read; only `gate_router_weight_decay`, default `0`) | Same as Exp3 (**inert**) |
| Gradient clipping | None (`max_grad_norm: null`) | Global `1.0` | Global `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1`, per-group `None`) | Same as Exp3 |
| z-loss | `1e-4` | `0.0` | `1e-4` | Same as Exp3 |
| Stored parameters | **BF16, no FP32 master** (`params=bfloat16`, device mode, `offload_opt_state: true`) | **FP32** (`params=float32`) | **FP32** (`p=f32, c=bfloat16`) | **FP32** (`p=f32, c=bfloat16`) |
| Batch / context / updates | `256 × 262k`; 746 updates | `256 × 262,144`; 204 updates | `256 × 262,144`; 388 of 746 updates | `256 × 262,144`; 360 updates |
| Loss mask | **All-token** (all 216 SFT + 1,711 pretrain children `format: text`) | SFT `serialized_chat` assistant-only; pretrain all-token | Per-source sidecar (`source_loss.json`: `chat_assistant_only` or `full_token`; per-source values not checked) | Same mechanism as Exp3 |
| Packing | Pack, block cross-doc | Cap `256` | Cap `256`, lookahead `128` | Same as Exp3 |
| Data catalog | 10/05 full mixture (`2026.10.24.2`, 377 components) | Same 377 components | Launch-input release URI (not visible in source) | V7 option-g |

Notes from the source read:
- **Inert / unchanged settings excluded from arms:** weight decay `0.1` in Exp3/Exp4 has no effect in `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py`, and z-loss is `1e-4` in both Exp1 and Exp4.
- **Interaction with issue 11793:** Exp1 used the same `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py` parameter routing (`4-D` routed expert banks on Adam, stacked norm scales on Muon-H) that hangs on update 1 under FP32 stored weights on the current long-loop runtime (issue 11793). Exp1 itself stored BF16 parameters with no FP32 master and therefore never exercised that FP32 path.

## Proposed one-at-a-time arms

All arms train SFT only on the fixed 10/05 full-mixture data from the pre-train Snowball base (one-hour scale first, then 8-hour scale), scored on Micro210 and the edit-call eval. Each non-baseline arm changes one verified Exp1-to-Exp4 setting:

| Arm | Single change from Exp1 baseline | Baseline (Exp1) value | Treatment (Exp4 / Exp2) value | Dependency / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | None (Exp1 SFT settings on fixed 10/05 mix) | `grug_moe_muonh_v1` (Adam experts, Muon-H norms), LR `5e-5` constant, no clip, BF16 params, all-token mask, no 256 cap | — | Reference point; precision choice interacts with issue 11793 |
| **1. Stored precision** | Stored parameter dtype | BF16, no FP32 master | FP32 (`p=f32, c=bfloat16`) | Blocked on issue 11793 for Exp1 optimizer routing |
| **2. Optimizer routing** | 4-D expert banks & norm scales assignment | `grug/moe/optimizer.py` (Adam experts, Muon-H norms) | `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py` (Muon-H experts, Adam norms) | Keep BF16 params for a single-knob contrast vs. Baseline; an FP32 variant can also run immediately (not affected by issue 11793) as a combined precision + routing check, while isolating routing on FP32 waits on Arm 1 / issue 11793 |
| **3. Adam-group LR & betas/eps** | Adam-group peak LR, betas, and eps | `5e-5`, optimizer defaults (`0.9 / 0.95 / 1e-8`) | `1.1538e-5` (`5e-5 × 3/13`), `0.9062 / 0.95 / 3.83e-15` | Tests lower Adam-group LR (most meaningful paired with Arm 2's group assignment as well) |
| **4. Gradient clipping** | Global gradient norm clip | None (`max_grad_norm: null`) | `global_gradient_clip = 1.0` | Direct single-knob switch |
| **5. LR schedule** | Decay schedule across the run | Constant `5e-5` (475-step decay tail unreached) | Linear decay to `0.1×` over the full run (Exp4) | Can optionally include cosine decay (Exp2) if linear moves the score |
| **6. Loss mask** | SFT token loss masking | All-token (`format: text`) | SFT assistant-only (`serialized_chat`), pretrain all-token | Verify Exp3/Exp4 `source_loss.json` per-source values before finalizing |
| **7. Packing cap** | Per-pack document cap & lookahead | No 256-doc cap | Cap `256` (lookahead `128`) | Direct single-knob switch |

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Scale difference from Exp1–Exp4 and Arm 1 dependency**

## Scale comparison

Our one-at-a-time SFT ablations run at 1/8th the per-update batch size of Exp1–Exp4:

| Setting | Exp1–Exp4 runs | Our 64-H100 ablations |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | 32 hosts × 8 H100 (256 H100 in Exp1) | 8 hosts × 8 H100 (64 H100; mesh `context=8`, `data=8`) |
| Packed rows per update | 256 (`256 × 262,144` = 67,108,864 tokens) | 32 (`trainer.trainer.train_batch_size: 32`; `32 × 262,144` = 8,388,608 tokens, 1/8×) |
| Microbatch / accumulation | — | `gradient_accumulation_steps: 4` (4 microbatches of 8 rows scanned inside one update; loss divided by the full 32-row scored-token count, `_accumulated_loss_and_grads` at commit `3b291b10`) |
| Updates per run (`stop_after_steps`) | 204 (Exp2), 360 (Exp4), 388 (Exp3), 746 (Exp1) | 150 (one-hour size); 500 (8-hour size) |
| Raw tokens per run | 13.69 B (204 updates) to 50.06 B (746 updates) | 1.26 B (150 updates, 4,800 rows); 4.19 B (500 updates, 16,000 rows) |

Because both batch size per update (8×) and total trained tokens are smaller than Exp1–Exp4, effects that depend on batch size or longer training horizons may differ between the one-hour screen, the 8-hour screen, and 256-H100 scale.

## Arm 1 dependency

Arm 1 (changing stored parameter precision from BF16 to FP32 under Exp1's optimizer routing, with 4-D routed expert banks on Adam and stacked norm scales on Muon-H) waits on issue 11793 (first-update hang under that combination on the current long-loop runtime). Isolating optimizer routing on FP32 likewise waits on issue 11793, while the BF16 single-knob arms and an FP32 combined precision-plus-routing check do not hit issue 11793.

This is a multi-run experiment with no results yet. The historical comparison also changes RL duration (16 versus 36 updates), so SFT-only scores cannot by themselves explain the post-RL gap. [#11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687) documents the BF16 stored-parameter caveat in the Exp1-style baseline; [#11793](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793) blocks the FP32 plus Exp1-routing comparison on the current runtime. The Exp3/Exp4 supervision sidecar is hash-pinned in [`exp3_recipe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1be0454367925411db6a432da3f62901881f8152/experiments/post_training/long_loop/exp3_recipe.py#L114-L126), but its per-source loss modes still need to be checked against the intended mask arm.

## Plan

1. Freeze the pre-train checkpoint, 10/05 catalog, source-loss sidecar and hash, runtime revision, data order, update count, and evaluation policy. Inspect the sidecar's per-source modes and verify that each arm changes only its named setting. Split the proposed LR/betas/eps and packing-cap/lookahead arms; separate expert-bank and norm routing if those assignments can be varied independently.
2. Run a matched Exp1-style BF16 baseline and one-hour SFT screens with the same source weights, sampling seed, update count, and checkpoint steps. Record consumed token counts because packing and masking change them. Score each checkpoint on the same frozen Micro210 and edit-call evaluations. Repeat the baseline to measure run and evaluation variation before promoting an arm whose score change exceeds that spread.
3. Keep the FP32 plus Exp1-routing cell gated on #11793. Once update 1 completes reliably, run a matched precision × routing comparison, then take only the decisive settings to eight-hour, repeated SFT runs. Report both Micro aggregates, benchmark-level scores, coverage, edit-call scores, seeds, configs, and checkpoint links, including negative results.
4. For any SFT setting that plausibly explains the gap, continue a matched pair through the same RL recipe and number of updates. Compare the post-RL checkpoints under one evaluation policy before attributing any part of the Exp1-to-Exp4 post-RL difference to SFT.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Optimizer routing per recipe: Exp1's expert banks fall through to Adam**

Source-verified parameter routing across five recipes (Exp1, Exp2, Exp3/Exp4 Hero-EP, the 11-19 control at `6164fcbd`, and the 10/05 run). No claim is made here about which routing performs better.

Conventions used below: `learning_rate` drives Muon-H and AdamH; `adam_lr` drives Adam. "Per-group" clip means `max_grad_norm` applied separately inside each optimizer group; "Global" means one gradient-norm clip across all parameters.

## Cross-recipe overview

| Weight group | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`, `bcf85728`) | Exp3 / Exp4 (`facbad18`) & 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`, `1f9bb1af`) | Real 10/05 (`ce7c77a`, `11baea1f`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`, `AdamConfig`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expert banks (`w_gate`, `w_up`, `w_down`)** | **Adam** (4-D fall-through) | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Attention & shared-expert matrices | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Gated norms | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` | **Muon-H** (2-D match; no norm rule) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `embed_norm` / `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `output_proj` / LM head | AdamH | AdamH | AdamH | Adam |
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| Clipping | none | global 1.0 | none | global 1.0 |

Every recipe except Exp2 uses mixed routing, with `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate`, and `output_proj` routed the same way across all mixed recipes; Exp2 is the only recipe applying plain Adam uniformly to all parameters.

## Per-recipe routing tables (verified from source)

### (a) Exp1 (`9662fdba02`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `bcf85728`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:285-307`. The SFT runtime stacks transformer blocks (`Transformer.stacked_blocks: ArrayStacked[Block]`, `sft_runtime/model.py:1251, 1283`), turning `(E, D, I)` expert weights (`levanter/grug/grug_moe.py:389-392`) into 4-D `(L, E, D, I)` leaves.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam (`L291-297`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` (LM head) | AdamH (`L298-299`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| gated norms (`embed`, `attn`, `mlp`, `final`) | Muon-H (`L301-302`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| attention `w_q/k/v/o`, shared expert `w_*`, latent `w_*` (stacked 3-D) | Muon-H (`L303-304`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| **expert banks `w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down` (4-D)** | **Adam** (`L305` fall-through) | **`adam_lr`** | none |
| stacked RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` (2-D) | **Muon-H** (`L303-304`; no norm rule in this blob) | `learning_rate` | none |
| `embed_norm` and `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam (`L305`) | `adam_lr` | none |

`max_grad_norm: null` (`sft.yaml:75`) and blob `bcf85728` has no global clip option. Both `learning_rate` and `adam_lr` are `5e-5` (`sft.yaml:61, 73`), so the Adam fall-through changed the update rule for expert banks without changing their LR value.

### (b) Exp3 / Exp4 Hero-EP (blob `facbad18`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_hero_ep_muonh_v1`; mask at `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:308-327`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L314-315`) | `adam_lr = 5e-5 * 3/13 = 1.1538e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L316-317`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L319-320`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| any `.weight` (RMSNorm scales, ShortConv) | Adam (`L323-324`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| expert banks (4-D) and other 2/3-D matrices | Muon-H (`L325-326`; normalised per expert bank via `expert_normalization`, `L86-92`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Per-group `max_grad_norm` is `None`. Global `1.0` clipping is set outside the optimizer (`global_gradient_clip=1`, `exp3_recipe:138`) and applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`.

### (c) 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `1f9bb1af`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:339-363`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L345-351`) | `adam_lr` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L352-353`) | `learning_rate` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L355-356`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| `.weight` (norm scales) | Adam (`L357-358`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. expert banks | Muon-H (`L359-360`; 4-D banks use the hero backend with `expert_normalization: all_experts`, `use_syrk: true`, build `L263-297`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Clipping comes from `global_grad_norm: 1.0` applied once before all groups (`L329-337`); per-group `max_grad_norm` is `null`. Routing matches Hero-EP `(b)`, and both use `expert_normalization: all_experts` and `use_syrk: true` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:228, 230` defaults in Exp3/Exp4); they differ in LRs (`learning_rate` `2e-5` vs `5e-5`; `adam_lr` `2e-5` vs `1.1538e-5`), with `1f9bb1af` sending 4-D leaves through the hero backend and 2/3-D leaves through the generic backend.

### (d) Real 10/05 run (`ce7c77a`, HF model card revision `8c76b22a`)

Trainer `experiments/grug_sft/special_token_lr.py` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True` at `L334`); optimizer `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py` `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (blob `11baea1f`, not `bcf85728`).

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L306-312`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L313-314`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales | Adam (`L317-318`, `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) | `adam_lr` | none |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L320-321`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. **expert banks** | **Muon-H** (`L328-329`) | `learning_rate` | none |

Config sets `learning_rate=5e-5`, `adam_lr=5e-5`, `max_grad_norm=None` (`special_token_lr.py:361-373`) with no global clip. One extra rule scales updates to the 7 special-token rows of `token_embed` and `output_proj` by `×√32` after the optimizer (`special_token_train.py:498-505`).

### (e) Exp2 (`442bf9d878`)

Plain Levanter `AdamConfig` (`levanter/optim/config.py:503-535`) with a single group (no mask, no `multi_transform`): every parameter gets `clip_by_global_norm(1.0)`, then `scale_by_adam`, then `lr = 5e-5`. Weight decay is `0`, so the decay mask is unused.

## Evidence that Exp1's 4-D expert-bank fall-through was unintended

- **Docstring mismatch:** The same blob `bcf85728` lists `"MoE MLP"` under `muonh` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:215`).
- **`(2, 3)` rule vs. stacked 4-D banks:** The `ndim in (2, 3)` rule was written for the `grug/moe` template (`grug/moe/model.py`, `blocks: tuple[Block, ...]`), where expert weights are 3-D and match Muon-H. `sft_runtime/model.py` stacks blocks into `ArrayStacked[Block]`, making expert banks 4-D, and the mask in `bcf85728` was not updated for 4-D leaves.
- **Explicit 10/05 comment:** The 10/05 optimizer (`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py:322-327`, blob `11baea1f`) explicitly guards against this trap: *"plus 4D when use_array_stacked_blocks=True… Without including 4D, stacked expert weights fall through to adam"*.
- **Branch fix not in `main`:** Commit `02c96d8378` (2026-11-17, `"[grug] Preserve Muon state across expert routing"`, no commit message body) adds 4-D routing, the `.weight` → Adam rule, and `test_muonh_groups_match_hero_for_stacked_and_unstacked_models`. It is present in `6164fcbd` but **not in `main`**.
- **Still in `origin/main`:** `origin/main` (blob `81304114`, `L311`) still checks `ndim in (2, 3)`, so any stacked-block run on `main` using `grug_moe_muonh_v1` repeats Exp1's routing (which current recipes on `main` use it was not checked).
- Nothing found in source records the Exp1 fall-through routing as a deliberate choice.

## What Exp1 → Exp3 changed in optimizer routing

Moving from Exp1 (`bcf85728`) to Exp3 (`facbad18`) changed three optimizer behaviors together:

1. **Expert banks (`w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down`):** Adam → Muon-H (with per-expert-bank `expert_normalization`).
2. **Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)`:** Muon-H → Adam (via the `.weight` rule, and at `adam_lr = 1.1538e-5` instead of `5e-5`).
3. **Gradient clipping:** none → global norm clip `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1` in `exp3_recipe:138`, applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`).

## Unverified detail

How generic Muon (`_grug_scale_with_muon`) handles Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales was **not traced or verified**. As a 2-D leaf they may be orthogonalised across layers as a single matrix, so that behavior is left open rather than stated as fact.

## Open question for experiment owners

Was Adam on the 4-D expert banks (and Muon-H on stacked RMSNorm scales) in Exp1 intended, or an unintended result of stacking blocks under the `ndim in (2, 3)` rule?

| updates where clipping changed the update (a group norm above 1.0) | 14 of 150 (updates 1-7, 9, 10, 13, 71, 101, 117, 144) | none (no clip) |
| train loss, update 150 | 0.4726 | 0.4727 |
| train loss, mean of updates 141-150 | 0.6721 | 0.6721 |

- **How clipping works here:** the optimizer (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`) clips each of its three parameter groups to norm 1.0 separately, not the total norm. In the step-150 checkpoint manifest (`opt_state`), the groups hold these parameters: AdamH holds `output_proj`; Adam holds `token_embed`, `embed_norm`, `final_norm`, the routers, router bias, attention gates and the expert MLPs (`expert_mlp` w_gate and w_up stored as `[26, 256, 2560, 1280]`, w_down as `[26, 256, 1280, 2560]`); MuonH holds the other matrices, the gated norms and the stacked `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp` weights (stored as `[26, 2560]`). So the binding count uses the group norms. In the clip run, the MuonH group was above 1.0 on 8 updates, AdamH on 13 and Adam on none. Nearly all of it is the first 13 updates plus 4 later spikes.
- **Where the numbers come from:** W&B logs `grad/norm/<parameter>` before the optimizer, so these are pre-clip norms. Each group norm is rebuilt from the 27 logged per-parameter norms, using the optimizer's own grouping rule. Their sum of squares matches the logged `grad/norm/total` within 1% on every update.
- **The loss curves are not equal step by step.** They differ on every one of the 150 updates, starting at update 1 by 0.00004 (0.79061 vs 0.79058).
  - Update 1's loss is computed before any update, so clipping cannot explain that first gap. It comes from the different cluster and executable, not from clipping.
  - Clipping can act from update 2 on. Mean absolute gap over updates 2-150 is 0.00034, and 12 updates differ by more than 0.001. The largest gap is 0.0044, at update 79, where the no-clip run had its one large spike (MuonH group norm 9.00 and Adam group norm 1.50, against 0.23 and 0.06 in the clip run).
- **Reading, not a conclusion:**
  - Clipping bound on 14 of 150 updates, mostly in the first 13. Train loss ended the same to the third decimal.
  - On held-out sets, no clip is 0.003-0.005 lower on all, SFT and SFT macro than clip 1.0. Replay pretrain, Nemotron and agenttrove are within 0.001.
  - Identity-data is 0.047 lower without clipping. It rests on 8 held-out packed sequences, and every arm drew 3 identity sequences in training (method caveat: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11783#issuecomment-7056481299).
    - **Correction (21 Nov):** updated the identity draw count from `1` → `3` packed sequences in 150 updates; the earlier realized-mix tool listed data sources in sorted order, whereas training uses config order (`MixtureDataset` insertion order).
  - These are single runs. The clip pair also crosses clusters, so a 0.003 gap is not separable from cross-cluster numeric noise without a repeat.
- **Weights:**
  - control (LR 2e-5): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-20261118/control-eager/checkpoints/step-150` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-20261118%2Fcontrol-eager%2Fcheckpoints%2Fstep-150))
