comments.body:
🤖 The public checkpoints test the hypothesis in the BF16-vs-FP32 comment and settle the unverified detail. Exp1 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round1-2026.11.12.7` (`475ba62d`), Exp2 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round2-2026.11.14.13` (`6546ba2d`) and Exp3 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round3-2026.11.17.55` (`8e787c61`). Each is compared with the base `open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8` (`3bbf729f`), so the numbers include each round's RL updates.

**BF16 storage rounded away most of Exp1's Muon-H updates.** After 746 SFT updates at 5e-5, 77% of Exp1's attention values are bit-identical to the base and 17% differ by one BF16 step. The Muon-H matrices moved 0.20%, and most of that is the hyperball re-projection rounding the stored values, `bf16(bf16(x / n) * n)`, which #11755 removes: measured from the re-projected base, they moved 0.125%. With FP32 storage, Exp2 and Exp3 moved the attention matrices 3.26% and 1.02%.

**The unverified detail.** On Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales, the Muon-H step left nothing that BF16 storage kept. 13.1% of the 133,120 scale values changed, 95.4% of the changed values equal what the re-projection alone gives from the base, and 99.5% of the values that the re-projection flips are flipped. The re-projection takes `n` over the whole leaf: `input_layernorm` (26 × 2560) needs `n = 336`, and its float64 norm is 335.03. What the orthogonalized step itself did stayed below one BF16 step, so the weights cannot show it.

**Where each round's update landed** (displacement `|round − base| / |base|` per class, then the share of values that changed):

| tensor class | Exp1 (BF16 storage) | Exp2 (FP32, Adam on all) | Exp3 (FP32, Hero-EP routing) |
|---|---|---|---|
| routed expert banks | 9.79%, 85.4% (Adam) | 3.60%, 94.9% | 0.79%, 76.7% (Muon-H) |
| attention q, k, v, o | 0.20%, 22.8% (Muon-H) | 3.26%, 93.9% | 1.02%, 82.1% |
| shared expert | 0.20%, 24.1% (Muon-H) | 3.40%, 94.7% | 1.06%, 83.7% |
| GatedNorm projections | 0.22%, 26.5% (Muon-H) | 3.24%, 95.0% | 1.10%, 83.3% |
| `lm_head` | 1.15%, 9.3% (AdamH) | 3.97%, 96.4% | 1.32%, 78.4% |

Exp1 is the only round whose always-active matrices barely moved, while its Adam fall-through moved the expert banks 9.79%. So Arm 1 (FP32 storage) and Arm 2 (expert banks on Muon-H) also change where the update lands, and a per-class displacement count of each arm's checkpoint against the base shows that before any eval. Method: #11687 and #11639.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body: 🤖 Arm C's drop matches what BF16 storage did to Exp1 (my comment above): a stored BF16 weight changes only when a step exceeds half a BF16 step, so smaller steps are lost at every update and never accumulate. On Exp1, after 746 updates at 5e-5, 77% of the attention values were still bit-identical to the base and the Muon-H matrices moved 0.20%, mostly the re-projection's rounding, while the Adam-updated expert banks moved 9.79%. If arm C's optimizer layout matches Exp1's, its attention, shared-expert and GatedNorm matrices have barely moved by step 150, so arm C differs from the control in which parameters trained, not only in storage precision. The finish reasons point the same way: 180 tool-call finishes against 908. Counting, per parameter class, the values in arm C's export that are bit-identical to its start checkpoint would confirm or rule this out in a few CPU minutes, without another eval.

The equal-weight gap (-4.87 pp) is larger than both repeat spreads, but the no-clip second repeat (50.16%) is within 1.76 pp of the lower clip-1.0 repeat (51.92%). The two clip-1.0 repeats above are the second run and the re-run; the failed run contributes no score.

## All 20 sources
No equal-20 headline: Harbor prepare failures are not comparable across the pair. Harbor trials scored of 100 per repeat: no clip 100 and 99; clip 1.0 97 and 98. Excluded trials count 0 in score and mass.

## Optimizer: arm E r2 (MoE expert banks on Adam) vs the 19 Nov control at seed 0 and seed 2, held-out loss (one hour, step 150)

All runs use the 19 Nov / 6164 data and model, FP32 stored weights, 20.47% replay and 150 updates. The score is all-token held-out loss, and the scorer loads FP32 params. Each run was scored in the cluster it was trained in, with the same eval config. Each cell is one training run.

**No control matches arm E r2 in both seed and cluster.** Arm E r2 was trained with seed 0 on cw-rno2a. The seed-0 control has the same seed but was trained on cw-us-east-02a. The seed-2 control was trained on the same cluster (cw-rno2a) with another seed. The two controls differ from each other by +0.0121 on held-out SFT (seed 2 − seed 0); read arm E r2's gaps against that spread.

## Optimizer groups

Read from the optimizer state saved in each step-150 checkpoint.

- **Control (both seeds):**
  - Muon-H on 18 arrays: attention w_q, w_k, w_v, w_o; MoE expert banks w_gate, w_up, w_down; shared MLP w_gate, w_up, w_down; GatedNorm w_down and w_up in the embed, attention, MLP and final GatedNorms.
  - AdamH on output_proj.
  - Adam on 8 arrays: token embedding, embed norm, attention RMS norm, attention gate, MLP RMS norm, router, router bias, final norm.
- **Arm E r2:** the three MoE expert banks (w_gate, w_up, w_down) move from Muon-H to Adam. The setting is `optimizer.muonh_param_ndims = [2, 3]`, so the 4-D bank arrays leave Muon-H.
  - Muon-H on the other 15 arrays.
  - AdamH on output_proj.
  - Adam on 11 arrays: the same 8 plus the three expert banks. The banks use the control's Adam settings: Adam learning rate 2e-5, beta1 0.9062, beta2 0.95, epsilon 3.83e-15.
- **All runs:** the global gradient norm is clipped to 1.0. Learning rates, schedule and weight decay are equal.

## Other config differences

Bookkeeping below means run ids, tracker names, and log, checkpoint, timing and sharding-dump paths.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 Arm F splits the two ways Adam differs from Muon-H on the banks. It keeps the per-coordinate normalization and drops the momentum, and it lands with arm E: Micro210 49.57% against 50.19%, +22.81 and +23.42 pp over the matched control. Its SFT loss sits between the two (0.536 against 0.488 for arm E and 0.648 for the control), so momentum may add a little, but most of the gain comes without it. That leaves the size of the step.

At the same rate the two kinds of rule take very different steps on a bank. Adam and the RMS rule scale each coordinate by the running RMS of its own gradient, so one update moves each coordinate by up to about the rate, 2e-5. Muon-H's hyperball update moves a bank by the rate times its Frobenius norm, which is 2e-5 × RMS(W) per coordinate. In the public long-loop base (`open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`) the routed experts have RMS(W) = 0.00975, so if the banks these arms start from are of that scale, the Muon-H step is about 100 times smaller per coordinate, and 150 updates move a bank by at most 0.3% of its norm. Exp1's Adam-updated banks show the full-size steps: on values below 2^-9, where BF16 rounding does not interfere, their RMS change is 1.34e-3, and 746 full-size steps of 5e-5 with uncorrelated signs give 5e-5 × √746 = 1.37e-3.

If the step size is the cause, Muon-H banks with a bank-only rate near 2e-5 / 0.00975 ≈ 2e-3 should close most of the gap. One more one-hour arm like E and F would test it, and would show whether the banks need a different rule or only a larger step.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖

## Mochi Bank-RMS probes: the line stops

We ran short probes of the RMSProp-style expert-bank rule on Mochi. The rule keeps a second moment only and has no momentum. Each probe restored Mochi's step-400407 SFT checkpoint and ran 20 updates (400407..400426). The reference twin is the production Muon-H run from the same checkpoint. All runs share update 400407, so the means below cover the 19 updates after it (400408..400426).

The rule was written before the last probe ran: mean loss within 1.05x of the twin, and no grad norm above 5.

| probe | mean loss, 400408..400426 | ratio to twin | grad norm | written rule |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Twin (Muon-H, production) | 0.483053 | 1.000 | 0.35 to 1.26 | reference |
| Control v2 (Muon-H banks, probe commit) | 0.483036 | 1.000 | max 0.737 | pass |
| Bank-RMS, cold start (bank state zero, full LR) | 0.828535 | 1.715 | 218.67 at 400413 | fail |
| Bank-RMS, warm second moment (20 warm-up passes, full LR) | 0.629574 | 1.303 | 136.21 at 400415 | fail |
| Bank-RMS, warm second moment, 0.25x bank LR | 0.521396 | 1.079 | 10.44 at 400409, 5.88 at 400413 | fail |

## What the probes show

- **Code ruled out.** Control v2 ran the same commit as the cold probe, with Muon-H on the banks. It matched the twin (1.000x, no spike at 400413). So the gap in the cold probe comes from the bank rule with fresh state, not from the newer code base.
- **The cold start is not the main cause.** Warming the second moment removed the 400413 spike (loss 0.667 against 3.711 cold). Most of the gap stayed: 1.29x the twin without 400413, against 1.38x cold.
- **Warm start plus a 0.25x bank LR is still 1.079x the twin and unstable.** All 19 updates are above the twin (1.014x to 1.261x per update). The grad norm passes 5 twice.
- **Snowball is not a like-for-like guide.** In Snowball, the bank arms were ahead of their own controls from update 1 (loss ratio 0.984 at update 1 in all three pairs). Their mean loss ratios over updates 2..20 were 0.913, 0.954 and 0.922; the one with the same RMSProp-style rule was 0.954. But each Snowball pair is two cold starts from the pre-train base with every optimizer slot fresh. Mochi sets a fresh bank state against a warm Muon-H twin mid-schedule.

## Decision

- Under the written rule, the Mochi Bank-RMS line stops here. There will be no 8-hour Mochi Bank-RMS run.
- A like-for-like test would need a fresh-optimizer start from Mochi's pre-train base.

## Result

At 8 hours (500 updates, step 500, cw-rno2a), we compare **arm F** (4-D expert banks on an RMSProp-style rule, second moment only, no momentum) with **arm E r2** (expert banks on Adam) and the **20.47% control** (Muon-H on every matrix).

- **Edit-call:** arm F is lower than both on sampled tool-call and applied-edit rates, with non-overlapping intervals (pooled applied edits 0.674 vs 0.825 for arm E r2 and 0.765 for the control). Most of that gap is replies with no parsed edit call. On greedy, the intervals overlap except strict format against the control.
- **Micro210** (14 clean sources, two repeats): arm F is 50.51% (47.97% / 53.05%), 7.19 pp below arm E r2 (57.70%) and 5.33 pp above the control (45.18%). Both gaps are larger than the 4 pp we read as one-run noise. Against arm E r2, both arm F repeats are below both arm E r2 repeats. Against the control, the gap is about the size of the repeat spreads (5.07 and 5.01 pp), so the repeats do not separate clearly.

- **Where the mass gap sits:** TriviaQA +1.50; OlympiadBench, GPQA, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro and HumanEval+ +1.00 each; CRUXEval +0.50; IFBench −1.00; AIME24 −3.50.
- **All 20 sources:** P1 41.46%, arm E r2 40.14% (+1.31 pp), plain 10% 23.17%. The excluded Harbor trials differ (P1 1 and 1; arm E r2 5 and 3), so this pair is not clean.
- **Length:** P1 averages 9,138 and 9,040 response tokens per sequence (arm E r2 8,970 and 9,006; plain 10% 7,755 and 7,534).

## Limits

- One training run per model. The edit-call intervals cover file-level sampling only, and the two Micro210 repeats cover inference only; neither measures training-seed variation. The held-out losses have no interval.
- P1 and arm E r2 differ in the replay share and the training code; the two cannot be separated here.
- The plain 10% run differs in the bank rule, the recipe and the cluster.
- One-hour rows only.

issues.title: [long-loop] Which Exp1-to-Exp4 SFT changes cost general and agentic ability?

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** The 10/05 SFT run and the Mochi Hero SFT both drew about 20% of their packed rows from pretraining replay (20.35% and 20.43%). Nobody had tested whether a different replay share gives a better model. The answer sets the data mix for Mochi's single SFT run.

- **Goal:** Find which pretraining-replay share gives the best Snowball SFT model when training from the pre-train base, at a fixed number of drawn rows.

- **Data:** The long-loop SFT mixture: 216 SFT stores (184 SFT sources) plus 193 pretraining-replay sources. Each run changes only the replay share; proportions inside the replay side and inside the SFT side stay fixed. Held-out loss uses 15 fixed sets: 11 SFT carve-outs (disjoint from training by construction) and 4 pretraining-replay validation sets. A one-hour run draws 4,800 rows, so small SFT sources are drawn rarely or not at all. For example, identity-data (0.03% of the mix) gets 0 to 3 sequences in a one-hour run.

- **Method:**
  - **19 Nov / 6164 recipe** (FP32 stored weights, expert banks on Muon-H). One-hour runs (150 updates, step 150) at 5%, 10%, 20.47% (the control), 40% and 60% replay, all seed 0 and trained on cw-us-east-02a, plus a seed-2 run of the 20.47% control, trained on cw-rno2a with a first-step barrier the seed-0 runs lack. Eight-hour runs (500 updates, step 500) at 10%, 20.47% and 40%, all seed 0: 10% and the 20.47% control (the same-cluster control of 22 Nov) were trained on cw-rno2a with the barrier, and 40% on cw-us-east-02a. An earlier eight-hour 20.47% run, trained on cw-us-east-02a, is kept for reference in the eight-hour bullets.
  - **18 Nov recipe** (BF16 stored weights; 18 Nov baseline: expert banks on Adam, norm scales on Muon-H; see issue 11858). One-hour runs at 10% and 40% (trained on cw-rno2a) and the 20.47% control (trained on cw-us-east-02a), all at seed 0. A second seed (seed 2) of the 10% and 20.47% runs, both trained on cw-rno2a.
  - **Mochi** (step 401600, GB200): eight-hour runs from the step-400407 checkpoint at 5% and 20.47% replay (the 20% arm's pretrain weight is 0.204734375), one run each, scored on cw-us-east-08a with the edit-call eval and the launcher evals (first 100 items, one seed), against the step-400407 baseline.
  - **Measures:** held-out loss (one forward-only scoring job per checkpoint), the edit-call eval (greedy, and five sampled seeds pooled), and Micro210 (two inference repeats of one checkpoint). Capability scoring clusters differ between some comparisons; each result line names them.
  - **Every point is one training run.** Inference repeats and file-level intervals do not measure training-seed variation. The seed-2 runs (the 18 Nov pair and the 19 Nov one-hour control) are the only repeats of a training run.

- **Results:**
  - **Held-out SFT loss, 19 Nov recipe, one hour** (5 / 10 / 20.47 / 40 / 60%): 0.6275 / 0.6570 / 0.6354 / 0.6633 / 0.6903. It is lowest at 5% and highest at 60%. The 10% run breaks the order, mostly through identity-data (2.149 at 10% vs 1.87 at 20.47%). That source has 8 held-out sequences, and the 10% run drew 1 identity sequence in training against 3 for the 5% and 20.47% runs. The seed-2 control (trained on cw-rno2a) is 0.6475. Of the other 9 SFT source sets, 8 are lower at 10% than at 20.47%.
  - **Held-out replay pretrain loss, same runs:** 0.8549 / 0.8544 / 0.8538 / 0.8533 / 0.8531. It falls slightly as replay rises; the whole spread is 0.0018. The step-0 base is 0.8561. The seed-2 control is 0.8536.
  - **Eight hours, step 500:** held-out SFT loss is 0.5348 at 10% and 0.5413 at 20.47% (the same-cluster control of 22 Nov; both trained on cw-rno2a, from different code commits), and 0.5913 at 40% (trained on cw-us-east-02a). Replay pretrain loss is 0.8523, 0.8515 and 0.8506, all below the base. No run shows a rise in replay loss up to 500 updates. This bullet earlier used the cw-us-east-02a 20.47% run (SFT 0.5414, replay 0.8515).
  - **18 Nov recipe, one hour:** held-out SFT loss is 0.5093 for the control, 0.5429 at 10% and 0.5552 at 40%. Replay pretrain loss is 0.8514, 0.8525 and 0.8513. Most of the SFT gap is identity-data (+0.42 for both replay runs). In training, the control drew 3 identity sequences and each replay run drew 1.
  - **Second seed, 18 Nov recipe, one hour (10% vs 20.47%):** at seed 2, held-out SFT loss is 0.5005 at 10% and 0.5099 at 20.47% (10% lower by 0.0094). At seed 0 the 10% run was 0.0337 higher than the control. Most of the seed-0 gap was identity-data (+0.4167); at seed 2 the identity-data gap is −0.0601. Each seed-2 run drew 2 identity sequences, against 1 (10%) and 3 (control) at seed 0. Without identity-data, the SFT source macro is lower at 10% at both seeds (−0.0069 at seed 0, −0.0041 at seed 2). Replay pretrain loss is slightly higher at 10% at both seeds (+0.0010 and +0.0004). The two 10% runs differ by 0.0425 on held-out SFT, almost all of it identity-data. The seed-0 pair also differs by training cluster.
  - **Edit-call, 19 Nov recipe, one hour** (5 / 10 / 20.47 / 40 / 60%, all scored on cw-us-east-02a): pooled applied edits are 0.509 / 0.574 / 0.465 / 0.606 / 0.613; greedy applied edits are 0.766 / 0.807 / 0.649 / 0.801 / 0.813. The 20.47% control is the lowest on both. Every other share is higher; the 5% intervals overlap the control's, the 10% and 60% intervals do not on either measure, and 40% does not on pooled. Exact matches (pooled) stay between 0.074 and 0.081 at every share, with overlapping intervals. The seed-2 control (trained and scored on cw-rno2a) has pooled 0.533 and greedy 0.760: between the seed-0 control and the other shares on greedy, and above 5% on pooled. It differs from the seed-0 control in cluster and barrier as well as seed.
  - **Edit-call, 19 Nov recipe, eight hours** (all scored on cw-rno2a; 10% and the same-cluster 20.47% control of 22 Nov trained on cw-rno2a, 40% on cw-us-east-02a): greedy applied edits are 0.842 / 0.836 / 0.848 and pooled 0.759 / 0.765 / 0.731 at 10 / 20.47 / 40%. All intervals overlap. This bullet earlier compared 40% with the cw-us-east-02a 20.47% run: 40% was lower on all 10 rates (pooled applies 0.731 vs 0.781), with all 10 interval pairs overlapping.
  - **Edit-call, 18 Nov recipe, one hour:** 10% is lower than the control on all 10 rates (pooled applies 0.608 vs 0.653). All interval pairs overlap. The 40% run has pooled applies 0.650 and greedy applies 0.789 (control 0.731), with intervals overlapping the control's; it was scored on cw-rno2a, the control and 10% on cw-us-east-02a.
  - **Edit-call, second seed (18 Nov recipe, 10% vs 20.47%):** at seed 2, pooled applied edits are 0.694 at 10% and 0.727 at 20.47%; greedy 0.795 and 0.801. So 10% is lower at both seeds on applied edits (seed 0: 0.608 vs 0.653 pooled), with overlapping intervals. Both seed-2 runs were scored on cw-rno2a and both seed-0 runs on cw-us-east-02a, so seed-2 vs seed-0 levels mix seed and scoring cluster.
  - **Micro210, 19 Nov recipe, one hour** (14 non-agentic sources, all trained and scored on cw-us-east-02a): the equal-weight mean is 25.77% / 32.86% / 27.08% / 25.35% / 24.04% at 5 / 10 / 20.47 / 40 / 60%, and the 14-source mass is 85.06 / 98.12 / 86.29 / 79.74 / 69.82. The 10% gap over the control (+5.78 pp) is larger than both repeat spreads, and the repeats do not overlap. The 5% repeats straddle the control (the widest spread of the five shares, 7.13 pp). Both 60% repeats sit below both control repeats on mass; the 40% repeats overlap the control. The six Harbor sources are mostly unmeasured for 40% and 60% (sandbox capacity), so they cannot be compared. The 10% model was scored from a BF16 downcast of its FP32 training state; that downcast is attested by the selection chain only. The seed-2 control (cw-rno2a) is 26.76% (repeat spread 4.02).
  - **Micro210, 19 Nov recipe, eight hours (step 500):** on the 14 non-agentic sources, the equal-weight mean is 48.58% at 10% and 45.18% at 20.47% (the same-cluster control of 22 Nov; both trained and scored on cw-rno2a), and 44.01% at 40% (trained and scored on cw-us-east-02a). Repeat spreads are 3.47, 5.01 and 0.84 pp. The 10% and 40% repeats do not overlap; the 20.47% repeats overlap both. This bullet earlier used the cw-us-east-02a 20.47% run (44.26%; 40% was −0.25 pp, and the 14-source mass 114.39 vs 119.33).
  - **Micro210, 18 Nov recipe, one hour:** all-source mass is 152.35 at 10% vs 145.01 for the control, inside the 10% run's repeat spread. On the 14 non-agentic sources, the equal-weight mean is 53.26% vs 48.88%, a gap larger than both repeat spreads. The six Harbor sources go the other way (−2.15 mass). At 40%, the 14-source equal-weight mean is 45.03% (−3.84 pp, larger than both repeat spreads) and all-source mass is 134.51 (−10.50); AIME24 alone is −7.50 of the −8.88 mass gap on the 14 sources. The 10% and 40% runs were scored on cw-rno2a, the control on cw-us-east-02a.
  - **Recipe level:** the 19 Nov recipe scores far below the 18 Nov recipe on Micro210 (87.29 vs 145.01 of 440 for the two controls). The cause is not isolated.
  - **Mochi, eight hours (step 401600):** edit-call greedy applied edits are 0.959 at 5% and 0.947 at 20.47% (step-400407 baseline 0.918), and pooled 0.923 and 0.932 (baseline 0.931); all intervals overlap. Across the 10 usable launcher evals (100 items each, one seed), 5% and 20.47% differ by 0–4 points on 9 evals and by 6.9 points on MRCR (23.5% vs 30.4%). One training run per arm.

**Reviewed rows** (19 Nov recipe and Mochi; plots of the same rows are available on request):

  - **Not settled:** the capability measures disagree with each other and across training length. On the 19 Nov recipe at one hour, the 20.47% control is the lowest share on edit-call applied edits, and every other share is higher; at eight hours the edit-call intervals (all scored on cw-rno2a) overlap for 10%, 20.47% and 40%. On Micro210 at one hour, 10% is the highest share (clearly above the control), 5% does not separate from the control, and 40-60% are lower; at eight hours 10% is highest (48.58%) and its repeats do not overlap 40%'s, while 20.47% overlaps both. On the 18 Nov recipe, 10% is above the control on the 14 clean Micro210 sources but below it on edit-call applied edits at both seeds, and 40% is below the control on Micro210. The two 10% runs on the 18 Nov recipe differ only in seed, yet differ by 0.0425 on held-out SFT loss, almost all of it identity-data. That is larger than the 10% vs 20.47% gap at either seed. The 19 Nov recipe has one seed repeat (the one-hour 20.47% control, which also differs in cluster and barrier; Micro210 26.76% vs 27.08%); on the 18 Nov recipe, the seed-2 edit-call pair differs from seed 0 in scoring cluster as well as seed.
  - **Read as a decision (19 Nov recipe and Mochi):** on the capability measures, no row shows 20.47% clearly better than 10% at either length (where 20.47% is higher, eight-hour pooled applies 0.765 vs 0.759, the intervals overlap). On one-hour held-out SFT loss 20.47% is lower than 10% (0.635 vs 0.657), but that gap sits in the 8-sequence identity-data set; at eight hours 10% is lower (0.535 vs 0.541). 40% and 60% are not clearly better than 10% on any capability measure (edit-call intervals overlap, Micro210 is lower), and they have higher held-out SFT loss than 20.47% (one hour; eight hours for 40%, across clusters). On Mochi, 5% and 20.47% are within each other's intervals on edit-call and differ by 0–4 points on 9 of 10 usable launcher evals, by 6.9 on MRCR. This is a reading of the rows, not a choice of share.
  - **Not shown:** causes; seed-to-seed spread except for the 18 Nov 10% and 20.47% runs and the 19 Nov one-hour control; a same-cluster, same-code comparison across replay shares at eight hours; held-out or Micro210 rows for Mochi; behaviour beyond 500 updates.

## Design

Parent: [issue 11535](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535).

- **Start checkpoint:** Pre-train Snowball base (fresh optimizer state, FP32 stored weights, 2026-11-18 optimizer assignment and clipping).
- **Arms (one-hour screen):** Three matched-compute runs of 150 updates × 32 packed rows × 262,144 tokens (4,800 packed rows / 1,258,291,200 raw sequence positions each), varying only the live mixture sampling weights (preserving internal proportions within both the 193 replay components and the 184 SFT components):
  - 20.47% pretraining replay / 79.53% SFT (baseline mixture unchanged; doubles as the recipe check)
  - 40% pretraining replay / 60% SFT
  - 60% pretraining replay / 40% SFT
- **Row share vs. trained-token share:** Each drawn row has 262,144 tokens, so row share equals raw-position share. As configured and served, the SFT rows compute loss on all real tokens (system, user, and tool-result tokens included) except each row's last position and padding; no role-based mask exists in the data or the trainer, and whether that was intended is not documented in the repo. Replay rows have zero padding while SFT rows average 7.5–8.0% padding across the three arms, so replay's share of trained tokens sits slightly above its realised row share across the first 4,800 drawn rows:

| Target replay weight | Realised replay rows (of 4,800) | Replay share of trained tokens |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 20.47% | 954 (19.88%) | 21.15% |
| 40% | 1,855 (38.65%) | 40.65% |
| 60% | 2,826 (58.88%) | 60.77% |
- **Follow-up scale:** An 8-hour screen follows after the one-hour screen, gated on the 20.47% baseline arm not reproducing the weak 2026-11-19 control score.
- **Evaluation:** Micro210 (two repeats per arm) and the edit-call eval.
- **Fixed-budget scope note:** Because total drawn packed rows (raw sequence positions) and training compute are held fixed across arms, increasing replay row share proportionally reduces SFT row exposure and slightly increases total loss-bearing tokens per update (because SFT rows carry 7.5–8.0% padding while replay rows have zero padding); this experiment compares replay/SFT allocation at matched training compute rather than adding extra replay rows on top.
- **Recipe caveat:** On 2026-11-19, the from-base FP32 control scored 87.29 of 440 on Micro210 (87.30 and 87.28) against 145.01 (141.76 and 148.26) for the 2026-11-18 from-base control (cause not yet isolated). These replay-share runs therefore pin the 2026-11-18 optimizer assignment and clipping while keeping FP32 stored weights (issue 11687).

🤖 **Reviewed edit-call results (all three one-hour replay arms): 63 of 855 (20.47%), 69 of 855 (40%), and 64 of 855 (60%).**

## Edit-call results

Each arm trains 150 updates (4,800 packed rows of 262,144 tokens) from the pre-train Snowball base on the same FP32 fallback control recipe (`6164fcbd`, routed expert banks on Muon-H; switched after the 2026-11-18 optimizer assignment hung on update 1, issue 11793), exported to BF16 and served once for this eval. The 20.47% arm is the 2026-11-19 from-base control run (same recipe, source, and seed, run at a different time). The eval covers 11 tasks and 58 files (171 prompts per pass; 855 pooled across seeds 1–5; exact match after stripping trailing whitespace).

| Arm | Seed 0 (of 171) | Greedy (of 171) | Seeds 1–5 | Pooled seeds 1–5 (of 855) | Strict calls (of 855 / 171 / 171) | Applied edits (of 855 / 171 / 171) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---|
| 20.47% replay (2026-11-19 control) | 15 | 14 | 8, 14, 14, 13, 14 | 63 (.074; .045–.099) | 485 / 104 / 115 | 398 / 91 / 111 |
| **40% replay** | **14** | **19** | **10, 18, 15, 13, 13** | **69 (.081; .055–.113)** | **616 / 127 / 145** | **518 / 107 / 137** |
| **60% replay** | **12** | **18** | **15, 13, 10, 12, 14** | **64 (.075; .047–.101)** | **629 / 127 / 146** | **524 / 105 / 139** |

- **40% vs 20.47% pooled exact matches:** +6 (+0.70 pp), with 6 tasks up, 1 down, and 4 tied (per-task changes from −4 to +4).
- **60% vs 20.47% pooled exact matches:** +1 (+0.12 pp), with 4 tasks up, 4 down, and 3 tied (per-task changes from −2 to +3).
- **40% vs 60% pooled exact matches:** +5 (+0.58 pp), with 5 tasks up, 2 down, and 4 tied (per-task changes from −2 to +3). All intervals are a descriptive 95% bootstrap over the 11 tasks and overlap across all three arms.
- **Strict calls and applied edits vs exact matches:** both higher-replay arms emitted more strict edit calls (616 for 40% and 629 for 60%, against 485 for 20.47% pooled) and more applied edits (518 and 524, against 398), while exact matches stayed close (69 and 64, against 63); most of the extra applied edits differed from the target file (449 of 855 pooled for 40% and 460 of 855 for 60%, against 335 of 855 for 20.47%).

## Caveats

- **Base-stream exposure (at its real size):** base-stream exposure is unverified for every arm. Across the first 4,800 rows, the 40% arm drew 1,855 pretraining replay rows (38.65% of rows; 40.65% of trained tokens, about 2× the 20.47% arm's 954 rows) and the 60% arm drew 2,826 replay rows (58.88% of rows; 60.77% of trained tokens, about 3× the 20.47% arm's 954 rows, which were 19.88% of rows / 21.15% of trained tokens), so the unverified base-stream exposure caveat scales accordingly.
- **One run per arm and weak baseline recipe:** this compares one training run, one checkpoint export, and one serve per arm on a weak baseline recipe (the 2026-11-19 from-base control scored 87.29 of 440 on Micro210 against 145.01 for the 2026-11-18 control). With one training run per arm and overlapping task intervals, these three points do not establish a replay-share effect or optimum on edit calls.

🤖 **Method caveat for every one-hour replay number: a short run draws only a small, fixed slice of the data mix.** Counts below are reproduced with the loader's own code.

**Correction (21 Nov):** the earlier version of this note listed data sources in sorted order, whereas `MixtureDataset` assigns dataset indices in the training config's `data.components` insertion order (Snowball's config order is not sorted; Mochi's runtime payload order is sorted, so all six Mochi rows are unchanged). Old → new for Snowball: pretrain replay 1 h `514 / 1,008 / 1,974 / 2,945` → `452 / 954 / 1,855 / 2,826` and 8 h `3,326 / 6,508` → `3,188 / 6,305`; identity draws 1 h `1 / 1 / 0 / 1` → `1 / 3 / 1 / 0` and 8 h `3 / 2` → `5 / 2` (1 h range `0 or 1` → `0 to 3`); zero-draw SFT sources (of 184) 1 h `61 / 69 / 80 / 93` → `61 / 69 / 78 / 82` (overall 1 h `61-93` → `61-91`: Snowball `61-82`, Mochi `88-91`) and 8 h `30 / 33` → `28 / 36`; the same-map sequence order holds across both Snowball recipes (18 Nov and 19 Nov), not between Snowball and Mochi.

Training data is drawn in blocks of 64,000 packed sequences (262,144 tokens each). Each source gets an exact slot count per block, its weight × 64,000. Within a block the slots are shuffled once, with the data seed. A run reads the block from position 0.
- A Snowball one-hour arm reads 150 × 32 = 4,800 sequences, 7.5% of one block. An 8-hour arm reads 500 × 32 = 16,000 (25%).
- A Mochi one-hour arm reads 143 × 16 = 2,288 (3.6%). The 8-hour plan reads 1,193 × 16 = 19,088 (29.8%).
- All arms use seed 0. Arms with the same map read the same sequence order on both Snowball recipes, so those same-map Snowball arms are not independent samples of the mix. Mochi lists its components in a different order (sorted vs Snowball's config order), so its arms read a different order from a Snowball arm with the same map.

- **Groups:**
  - pretrain replay is `pretrain/*`;
  - Nemotron is `sft/source/nemotron_sft_v3/*`;

  - penfever traces is `sft/source/penfever-traces/*`;
  - identity is `sft/source/identity-data`;
  - other SFT is every remaining SFT source, including `sft/pooled`.
- **What it means:**
  - The large groups (pretrain replay, Nemotron, other SFT) land within 1.7 percentage points of nominal. The largest gap is still Mochi 20.47% 1 h pretrain replay, 22.12% vs 20.47% (the Snowball worst case is 40% 1 h pretrain replay, 38.65% vs 40.00%, 1.35 percentage points).

  - So per-source effects in one-hour arms, identity-data especially, reflect which few sequences were drawn, not the nominal weight.
- **How it was reproduced:**
  - It runs Levanter's own `MixtureDataset` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/mixture.py`, identical at Snowball pin 2d3a1574 and Mochi PR head 4540eedb) with placeholder datasets.
  - It uses each run's consumed `data.train_weights` (from the W&B config for Snowball and the frozen plan maps for Mochi), each run's submitted config component order (insertion order, which `MixtureDataset` keeps), block size 64,000 and the key `mix_key = split(split(PRNGKey(0), 2)[0])[0]`.
  - It reads `_get_block(0)` and decodes each slot id as `id >> 16`, the dataset index.
- **Self-check:** for every arm, the per-source counts over the full 64,000-slot block equal each source's slot count exactly. The script asserts this before counting.
- **Status:** reproduced with the loader's own code; the key path, component order, block assignment and batch-to-position mapping were checked against the pinned source. Pretrain-replay row counts match an independent count through the training data path (954 / 1,855 / 2,826 of 4,800); the runs log no per-source draws.
- **Mochi seed:** `trainer.seed` 0, `data_seed` None and `mixture_start_step` 400407 are read from each arm's frozen worker payload.
- **Packing:** packing differs between the Snowball and Mochi pins, so the counts are per source, not token-equal across stacks.

## Setup and scope

- **40% vs 20.47% at 8 hours:** 40% is lower than 20.47% on all 10 rows (greedy applies `−0.029`; pooled applies `−0.050`; pooled strict `−0.056`).
- **Interval overlap:** all 10 pairs of 95% file-level intervals overlap, so there is no clear separation at this sample size.

## Second seed: 10% vs 20.47% replay, 18 Nov recipe, one hour

(18 Nov baseline: expert banks on Adam, norm scales on Muon-H; see issue 11858.) All four runs store weights in BF16, and the scorer loads BF16 params. Each run is 150 updates (step 150). Each cell is one training run.

- **Seed 2:** both runs were trained on cw-rno2a. They differ only in replay share.
- **Seed 0:** the 10% run was trained on cw-rno2a. The 20.47% run is the 18 Nov control, trained on cw-us-east-02a. So the seed-0 pair also differs by training cluster.

## Held-out loss (lower is better)

| measure | seed 2: 10% | seed 2: 20.47% | seed 2: 10% − 20.47% | seed 0: 10% | seed 0: 20.47% (control) | seed 0: 10% − 20.47% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| held-out SFT | 0.5005 | 0.5099 | −0.0094 | 0.5429 | 0.5093 | +0.0337 |
| SFT source macro, without identity-data | 0.4726 | 0.4767 | −0.0041 | 0.4738 | 0.4806 | −0.0069 |
| identity-data | 1.0170 | 1.0770 | −0.0601 | 1.4594 | 1.0427 | +0.4167 |
| Nemotron macro | 0.4968 | 0.5011 | −0.0043 | 0.4981 | 0.5057 | −0.0075 |
| replay pretrain | 0.8516 | 0.8511 | +0.0004 | 0.8525 | 0.8514 | +0.0010 |
| identity sequences drawn in training | 2 | 2 | | 1 | 3 | |

Differences are computed from unrounded values. Identity draws are reviewed counts from each run's training order.

## Reading

- **Held-out SFT changes sign with the seed.** At seed 0, 10% was higher than 20.47% (+0.0337). At seed 2, 10% is lower (−0.0094).
- **Most of the seed-0 gap was identity-data** (+0.4167). Identity-data has 8 held-out sequences. At seed 0 the 10% run drew 1 identity sequence in training and the control drew 3. At seed 2 both runs drew 2.
- **Without identity-data, 10% is lower at both seeds:** −0.0069 at seed 0 and −0.0041 at seed 2 on the SFT source macro. Nemotron macro is also lower at 10% at both seeds.
- **Replay pretrain loss is slightly higher at 10% at both seeds** (+0.0010 and +0.0004).
- **Seed against seed:** the 10% runs differ by 0.0425 on held-out SFT (seed 2 lower), and almost all of that is identity-data. The 20.47% runs differ by 0.0007, but that pair also differs by training cluster.

## Limits

- Two seeds only. The seed-0 pair also differs by training cluster, so the seed and cluster effects cannot be separated there.
- These are held-out losses only. No capability eval has been run on the seed-2 models.
- These numbers do not show what caused any difference.

| | Equal-weight 14, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) | 14-source mass of 340, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) |

The equal-weight gap (+5.78 pp) is above both repeat spreads (4.74 and 4.37 pp), and the repeats do not overlap: the 10% lower repeat (30.49%) is 1.23 pp above the 20.47% upper repeat (29.26%). In mass both 10% repeats (92.45, 103.79) sit above both 20.47% repeats (86.30, 86.28), by 6.15 and 17.49 (against the upper control repeat, 86.30). 🤖

## Mochi launcher results: baseline, 20% replay and 5% replay on 13 evaluations

Three Mochi models, scored with the evaluation launcher from PR 11528 (head `b3611d8a`): the sealed step-400407 baseline, and the 20% and 5% replay models (8-hour arms, step 401600). Each model ran on its own vLLM server (16 GB200 GPUs, data parallel 16). These are launcher rows. Compare Mochi only with Mochi on this launcher.

## Row rules
- `--limit 100`: the first 100 source items of each evaluation (AIME24: 30 problems x 10 trials = 300 samples; GPQA-Diamond: 100 questions x 3 trials = 300). One trial per item elsewhere.
- Reply cap 16,384 tokens, 32 concurrent requests per evaluator, one evaluator at a time. Thinking on for AIME24, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro and MATH-500; off for the other nine.
- **A reply cut at its cap counts as wrong**, whatever letter or answer the grader extracted. The cap is 16,384 tokens, except CRUXEval (2,048) and NUPA5K-loose (256), whose tasks set their own. Unscored items would also count as wrong; none are unscored here.
- The launcher's own score is shown beside the capped score where they differ. It credits answers extracted from cut-off replies.
- Flags: 10% or more of replies cut at the cap means "cap-bound" and the row is not used to rank. If two models' cut shares differ by 5 points or more, the row is "cap-affected".

## Results (capped score; launcher score in brackets where different)

| Evaluation (items) | Baseline | 20% | 5% | Cut at cap (baseline / 20% / 5%) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIME24 (300) | 63.00% (64.33%) | 63.67% (64.67%) | 62.00% (63.33%) | 108 / 105 / 110 | cap-bound, unranked |
| GPQA-Diamond (300) | 57.67% (72.00%) | 61.67% (73.67%) | 58.67% (70.33%) | 108 / 104 / 108 | cap-bound, unranked |
| MMLU-Pro (100) | 61.00% | 67.00% | 63.00% (65.00%) | 3 / 2 / 4 | usable |
| MATH-500 (100) | 94.00% | 96.00% | 96.00% | 4 / 3 / 1 | usable |
| GSM8K 0-shot, flexible-extract (100) | 77.00% | 79.00% | 82.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable (strict-match is 0.00% for all three: its pattern never matches these replies) |
| TriviaQA, extract_answer (100) | 73.00% | 65.00% | 66.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| TruthfulQA, acc (100) | 70.20% | 70.62% | 70.35% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| HumanEval+ (100) | 85.00% | 89.00% | 90.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| MBPP+ (100) | 82.00% | 77.00% | 78.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| CRUXEval (100) | 90.00% | 87.00% | 84.00% (85.00%) | 2 / 4 / 3 | usable |
| IFBench, strict prompt (100) | 37.00% | 36.00% | 35.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| MRCR, accuracy (100) | 28.27% | 30.40% | 23.46% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| NUPA5K-loose, exact match (100) | 15.00% | 12.00% | 16.00% | 48 / 51 / 54 | cap-bound at its 256-token task cap, cap-affected, unranked |

Among the replies that were not cut, AIME24 is correct on 98.44% / 97.95% / 97.89% (baseline / 20% / 5%) and GPQA-Diamond on 90.10% / 94.39% / 91.67%. On GPQA-Diamond the launcher's own score credits 43 / 36 / 35 cut replies, which is why it is far above the capped score.

## Notes
- **Code evaluations.** In the first full runs, HumanEval+, MBPP+ and CRUXEval could not be graded on this branch: the grader's setup step ran before the answer file was installed (fixed on `main` by `1a8a628d26`, PR 11408). The three code rows come from reruns with that commit cherry-picked onto the PR head; the replies are fresh samples, not re-grades. All other rows come from the first runs on the PR head alone.
- **Replaced baseline run.** The first baseline rerun of the code evaluations was replaced: its server failed to start, so it was cancelled and launched again.
- **Transient errors.** A few single requests hit a connection error at the model call (MMLU-Pro once per model; also single items in GSM8K, TriviaQA and NUPA5K-loose in some runs). Each recovered on its first retry, and every item is scored in every row.

## What this does not show
- Each usable row is 100 items, one trial per item, one run per model, with no seed replicate (AIME24 and GPQA-Diamond run 10 and 3 trials per item, and are unranked). Differences of a few points are inside what one run of this size can resolve.
- AIME24, GPQA-Diamond and NUPA5K-loose are unranked, because 35 to 54% of replies hit their cap.
- It does not show why any model differs from another: nothing here separates training changes from sampling noise.

## Reading
On the usable rows the 20% and 5% models are mostly within a few points of each other (the largest gaps are MRCR, 30.40% vs 23.46%, and MMLU-Pro, 67% vs 63%), within what a single n=100 run resolves. Against the baseline, both 8-hour models score lower on TriviaQA (65% and 66% vs 73%), MBPP+ (77% and 78% vs 82%) and CRUXEval (87% and 84% vs 90%), and higher on HumanEval+ (89% and 90% vs 85%).

## Result

At one hour (150 updates, step 150, trainer seed 0), we compare three runs with expert banks on Adam, all trained and scored on cw-rno2a, that differ in the pretraining replay share: **r0** (0% replay), **P1** (10% replay) and the one-hour **arm E r2** (20.47% replay). The bank-optimizer results for P1 and arm E r2 are in issue 11858 (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7095004990).

- **Held-out loss:** r0's SFT loss is higher than both (0.5912 vs 0.5032 for P1 and 0.5016 for arm E r2). The identity-data set is much higher (2.3100 vs 1.2696 and 1.1933), while the Nemotron SFT v3 macro and agenttrove losses are slightly lower. On the pooled SFT loss, r0 is about equal (0.2228 vs 0.2255 and 0.2229). Its pretrain macro loss is slightly higher (0.8618 vs 0.8597 and 0.8578).
- **Edit-call:** The r0 and P1 intervals overlap for every reported rate (pooled applied edits 0.806 vs 0.774). r0 is higher than arm E r2 on every tool-call, parse, strict-format and applied-edit rate, with non-overlapping intervals (pooled applied edits 0.806 vs 0.642).

**Across the three measures:** Compared with P1, r0 had higher held-out SFT loss, with the largest increase on identity-data. All reported edit-call intervals overlapped, and r0 averaged 2.37 percentage points lower on equal-weight Micro210. Across the three replay shares, the Micro210 means are not monotonic (52.32%, 54.69%, 51.75%), so we claim no replay trend. Arm E r2 was trained on a different code commit, so gaps against it combine the replay share and the code. One training run per model.

## Setup

- All three: FP32 stored weights, 150 updates, trainer seed 0, expert banks on Adam, trained and scored on cw-rno2a.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Micro210 TruthfulQA rows list a correct answer as option A in every row, so a model that always answers "A" scores 1.0. The frozen prepared rows keep TruthfulQA's source order, which puts the true answers first. The Exp5 SFT step-527 Micro210 run scored 1.00 on `truthfulqa_truthful_qa`; earlier runs scored 0.90 and 0.70. These scores measure how often the model picks A.

Reproduce:
1. Read `rollouts.parquet` from `open-athena/micro210-prepared-tasks@d8fa0e259ae63b1978388b20a17f72036642dd05`.
2. Select the 10 rows whose benchmark is TruthfulQA.
3. Read the options in each prompt. Option A is a true answer in all 10, for example "A. It doesn't tell us anything about global warming." and "A. The word \"chav\" is not an acronym."

Expected: options are shuffled with a fixed, recorded seed per row, and the grader accepts only the shuffled letters of the true answers.

Done when:
- TruthfulQA option order in the Micro210 build is a seeded permutation, recorded per row, and the grader scores against the permuted letters.
- The other multiple-choice rows in Micro210 (GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro and any other lettered-choice benchmark) are checked for the same fixed-position bias, and fixed the same way where present.
- A regression test fails when the correct option sits at one fixed position for every row of a benchmark.
- The fix ships as a new Micro210 policy version. The frozen version is not edited in place, and the change note lists which benchmark scores change.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
### Summary
The SWE-bench-style shared graders (the taskcompendium log parsers behind the SWE_REBENCH profile) record reward 0.0 for rows whose full test suites PASS in an identical environment. The F2P/P2P parse fails to match the config's test ids against the suite output, so fully-passing suites score 0.0.

### Evidence (SWE-rebench V2.1 repaired wave, the sealed canonical)
The wave's oracle verdicts for three rows, compared against diagnostic runs of the SAME setup + gold patch + test command in the same environment family (the full captures linked below):

| instance | wave oracle reward | diagnostic run |
|---|---|---|
| blitz-js__superjson-78 | 0.0 | Test Suites: 8 passed, 8 total; Tests: 48 passed, 48 total |
| goplus__gop-1659 | 0.0 | 26 `ok` package markers, 0 `FAIL` |
| segmentio__encoding-45 | 0.0 | `--- PASS`, `PASS`, `ok` — 0 `FAIL` |

The suites are fully green; the recorded oracle rewards are 0.0.

### Suspected mechanism
The family config's test ids (FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS) are matched against the suite output by the taskcompendium log parser (parse_log_node for jest, the go-test parser for go). The parsed test names do not match the ids' form (the describe-block-qualified jest names vs the ids' form; the go package-level output), so the parse reports 0 matches and the reward collapses to 0.0.

### Reproduction
- The wave's ledger: s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/swe-repair/2026.11.20.1/wave-v11/fidelity-wave1-outcomes.json (the keys `<instance>|condensed|oracle`, reward 0.0).
- The diagnostic captures (the same setup + patch + test command, the full output): s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/swe-repair/2026.11.20.1/wave-v11/diagnose-blitz-js__superjson-78.txt (and the gop/encoding-45 siblings).

### Impact
The repair wave's oracle-failed tail (13,471 rows) includes a material share of such false negatives; the rows are graded 0.0 despite passing suites.

### Labels
agent-generated

comments.body:
🤖 Two results that may help while the wave's own trial files are pulled.

Full reruns agree with the replays above. With each row's gold patch and the dataset's test command, run through main's rendered `solve.sh`, `test.sh` and generated `grade.py` with the images' toolchain versions (Go 1.18.1; Node 16.20.2 with jest 24.9.0), all three rows score 1.0: `superjson-78` 31/31 F2P and 17/17 P2P, `gop-1659` 4/4 and 746/746, `encoding-45` 1/1 and 340/340. Without the gold patch each scores 0.0. The parsers find no ids only in other output forms: jest without `--verbose` (0 names), `go test` without `-v` (one package `ok` line, 0 names) and `go test -json` (341 names, each prefixed with the package path, so no id matches). No V2.1 Go row's `test_cmd` uses either Go form (2,168 of 2,269 pass `-v`; the other 101 run `make` or a script), so a `test_cmd` in the wave's `config.json` that differs from the dataset row is the first thing to check.

A runtime path zeroes `gop-1659` with no parse problem, if the wave graded through the shared-source controller of #11844 without network. That controller runs `test.sh` as UID 10002 with `HOME=/home/taskcompendium-grade` ([`runtime/shared_source.py` L494](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c35cd238310452c070a059e9d1fd81a1575362a9/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/shared_source.py#L494)). The gop image builds its module cache in `/root/go/pkg/mod` and keeps `/root` at mode 700, so `go` starts from an empty cache. With module downloads off, the gold patch fails to build (`module lookup disabled by GOPROXY=off` on every import), the log has no `--- PASS` or `--- FAIL` line, and the reward is 0.0; with a copy of the image's cache, still offline, it is 1.0. Of the 2,269 V2.1 Go rows, 2,030 leave the module cache under the build user's `HOME` (209 set a path outside it, 30 vendor their modules). The other two rows score 1.0 as UID 10002 with a fresh `HOME`, so this can explain gop only. A module download error in the wave's gop `test_output.log` would confirm it.

When reading those logs: the controller opens `test_output.log` as `test.sh`'s stdout without `O_APPEND` ([L496](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c35cd238310452c070a059e9d1fd81a1575362a9/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/shared_source.py#L496)), and `test.sh` writes the test output into the same file with `cat >`, so its `test_cmd exit code: N` line overwrites the first bytes of the test output before `grade.py` reads it. On these three rows those bytes are an `=== RUN` or header line, so no id is lost.

issues.author: chrismc91
issues.body:
`levanter.model_cache.cache_to_prefix` treats a mirrored model as present when its `.cache_metadata.json` marker exists. The mirror lives under a `ttl=14d` temp prefix, and the bucket lifecycle deletes the mirror's objects one at a time once they pass 14 days. For a while the marker survives while other files are already gone. The cache keeps reporting a hit, and vLLM fails at startup.

Seen on 2026-11-21 with `open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14`, mirrored on 2026-11-07 to `s3://marin-us-east-08a/tmp/ttl=14d/quick-serve-models/open-athena_Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14_6783e9743478bd25a9ce03ab3460e84d6a9814b0-e03552f6ec83663c/`. Two eval launches on `cw-rno2a` logged `model cache hit` for that path. vLLM then exited with:

```
Value error, Invalid repository ID or local directory specified: '/root/.cache/vllm/assets/model_streamer/45c77d7a'.
```

On 2026-11-21, listing the prefix showed `.cache_metadata.json`, `model.safetensors.index.json`, `tokenizer.json`, `tokenizer_config.json` and safetensors shards, but no `config.json`. All objects were written at 2026-11-07 00:38. The same launch config served this model successfully about 18 hours earlier, before the lifecycle reached it. By 2026-11-23 the lifecycle had removed the whole prefix, and the next launch re-mirrored the model.

The hit check is the marker-only `fs.exists(marker)` in `cache_to_prefix` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py:111`). `resolve_cached_model_path` uses the same check for `CacheMode.READ_ONLY`. Any model whose mirror outlives the TTL hits this for up to a day. Every launch fails until the lifecycle removes the marker, and only then does the next launch re-mirror.

One fix is to treat a marker older than the TTL minus a margin, say one day, as a miss and re-populate under the existing lock. That never serves a snapshot the lifecycle may be deleting. Checking that `config.json` exists would catch this instance, but not a deleted weight shard.

---

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`cache_to_prefix` treats an existing `.cache_metadata.json` as a hit even when bucket lifecycle has begun deleting the snapshot. `READ_ONLY` uses the same marker check. A refill also skips surviving files by size, so their original lifecycle age would still expire after the marker is replaced.

**Relevant code**
- [model_cache.py#L72-L143](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py#L72-L143) — marker checks and lock
- [model_cache.py#L179-L218](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py#L179-L218) — TTL resolution and read-only hit
- [model_cache.py#L250-L293](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py#L250-L293) — size-based reuse during refill

# Proposed Fix

The launcher resolves a 14-day cache path, `READ_ONLY` or `cache_to_prefix` sees the stale marker, and vLLM receives a partial snapshot. Treat markers near their lifecycle deadline as misses in both paths; under the existing lock, refill missing files and refresh the lifecycle age of surviving files before writing a new marker. Add local filesystem regressions for stale-marker refill and read-only fallback.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 Opened #12120 with `Fixes #12114`. Stale markers now trigger a locked refill or a read-only fallback, and surviving files have their lifecycle age refreshed before the new marker is written. The cache regressions and full pre-commit pass passed; the Levanter suite had 1,918 passes, 463 skips, and one xdist worker exit whose test passed alone.

issues.body:
Part of #9541. Before spending hero compute, validate the hinted eval (#11866) and the fit module (#11867) against the paper's published Delphi GSM8K results. This gate only checks our code; hero conclusions come from hero checkpoints.

Run GSM8K truncation and masking on the Delphi base checkpoints the paper used (`marin-community/delphi-*`, every published seed; see `docs/reproducibility/delphi-seed-repeats.md`). Use the first 256 test problems, 64 rollouts at H=0 and 32 at H>0, and seed means for the fit. Planning estimate: about 25 H100-hours.

Done when:
- Each of our truncation and masking accuracies lies inside the 95% bootstrap interval of the paper's curve.
- Our fit on the paper's ladder points reproduces the paper's forecast MAE within 1 pp: 3.1 pp for masking and 3.3 pp for truncation.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The released GSM8K/Delphi grid has 34 checkpoints and 6,127,616 no-hint, masking, and truncation rollouts. [#11866](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11866) and [#11867](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11867) remain open, with no matching implementation PR found. The paper's 3.1 pp masking and 3.3 pp truncation values are Table 1 *in-sample fit* MAEs averaged across Delphi and four post-trained families; they are not Delphi forecast MAEs. The released GSM8K hints retain `<<…>>` calculator annotations and hint the five-shot exemplars, while #11866 specifies removing the annotations.

**Relevant code**
- [Delphi checkpoint inventory](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/reproducibility/delphi-seed-repeats.md) — published seeds and repository names.
- [Paper GSM8K prompt and grader](https://github.com/tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws/blob/c0490e53ba8eae58bf5375f6b56956f0d57dad30/src/hinted/benchmarks/gsm8k_delphi.py) — exemplars, redaction, strict answer extraction.
- [Paper evaluation grid](https://github.com/tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws/blob/c0490e53ba8eae58bf5375f6b56956f0d57dad30/experiments/query_hinted_benchmarks/README.md) — checkpoint and rollout counts.
- [Released result format](https://github.com/tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws/blob/c0490e53ba8eae58bf5375f6b56956f0d57dad30/data/results/README.md) — problem-level outcomes and seeds.
- [Table 1 script](https://github.com/tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws/blob/c0490e53ba8eae58bf5375f6b56956f0d57dad30/experiments/forecasting/table1.py) — pooled fit MAE calculation.

# Proposed Fix

1. Complete #11866 and #11867 with a paper-compatible GSM8K variant. Pin the paper data/code revision and each checkpoint revision. Compare generated prompts against the released prompts, including calculator annotations, hinted exemplars, answer redaction, five-shot completion format, and the H=0 prompt. Match the paper's strict `####` grader, 512-token limit, temperature 0.4, and top-k 1000 for H>0 (off at H=0).
2. Run the fit module on the paper's released outcomes without GPUs. Reproduce the pooled Table 1 values as a software check; separately record the Delphi-only fit MAE, fitted parameters, and held-out forecast errors. Those Delphi values are the relevant fit targets for this gate.
3. Smoke-test two problems, then run one checkpoint on all 256 problems at H=0, 0.5, and 1 to verify grading, output records, and measured H100 throughput. Re-estimate the issue's 25 H100-hour budget from that pilot before submitting the full grid.
4. Run all 34 checkpoints on the first 256 test problems: 64 rollouts at H=0 and 32 for each method at H=0.1–1.0. Store checkpoint revision, training seed, problem ID, method, H, prompt version, rollout, and grade. Average seeds within each compute budget, then compare every accuracy with the released per-problem outcomes using problem-bootstrap intervals. Publish the curves, pointwise differences, fit results, and any protocol or grading discrepancies.

The issue's 3.1/3.3 pp acceptance target should be replaced with Delphi-specific fit values from the released data. Report both the requested paper-only 95% intervals and a two-sample bootstrap comparison; requiring every one of 252 point estimates to fall in a separate 95% paper interval creates false failures even under a matching protocol. Keep [#11869](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11869) gated on this result.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Mochi and Snowball long-loop RL need an ablated optimizer and learning rate. Since the 2026-11-23 normalization, both models use MuonH with `lr` 1e-5 and `adam_lr` 2.307692307692308e-6 (`offload_momentum: true`), `max_grad_norm` 0.5 and 64 prompts × 8 samples per batch. Snowball moved from AdamW to MuonH for memory: AdamW state did not fit at long context without CPU optimizer offload, and offload slowed each step. Neither the optimizer nor the learning rate came from an ablation. The earlier tuned Snowball RL comparison in #7786 (hypothesis V) found that AdamW learned faster and reached a higher peak training reward than MuonH. This experiment should settle both choices for each model. It is planned here and not yet scheduled.

Design:
- Curriculum: our best RL curriculum at the time it runs, identical for both models. Record its identity and version.
- Fixed settings: the normalized config for all other settings (staleness 3, 98,304-token response cap and 131,072-token context, batch 64 × 8, `max_grad_norm` 0.5), one seed per arm, and the frozen 200-row validation split from the curriculum.
- Optimizer arms: (a) MuonH with `offload_momentum: true` and the `adam_lr`/`lr` ratio held fixed; (b) AdamW with CPU optimizer offload. Each arm uses the qualified trainer layout for its memory profile.
- Grid per optimizer and model: half-decade steps. MuonH starts at 3e-6, 1e-5, 3e-5 and 1e-4. AdamW starts at 3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6 and 1e-5. Learning rates do not transfer between optimizers.
- Metric: an EMA of validation accuracy over the first 20 optimizer updates (EMA window 5, matching best-checkpoint selection). Report raw per-eval accuracy and training reward alongside it.
- Cost: report median seconds per update and GPU-hours per update for each arm, split into rollout wait, optimizer step and offload transfer. AdamW with offload wins only if its accuracy gain justifies its step-time cost.
- Adaptive grid: if the best arm of an optimizer is at either edge of its grid, add the next half-decade step beyond that edge and repeat until the best value is interior.
- Stability checks per arm: training/inference mismatch KL, gradient norm and the clipped-gradient fraction. Report any divergence as a result, not a rerun.

Done when:
- Each optimizer has a learning-rate curve per model whose best value is interior to its grid, with EMA validation accuracy at 20 updates and seconds per update per arm.
- A recommended optimizer and learning rate per model is stated, with the accuracy, cost and stability metrics that support it.
- The long-loop RL defaults are updated, or confirmed unchanged, from that recommendation.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A SkyRL evaluation on `cw-us-east-02a` selected Ethernet/RoCE HCAs and failed its launch-time collective gate on all 16 hosts.

Reproduce:
1. Submit a 16-node, 8-H100-per-node SkyRL generation job to `cw-us-east-02a` without an explicit `NCCL_IB_HCA` in the child request.
2. Run the standard all-GPU interconnect gate with the task runtime.
3. Inspect the per-task port inventories and retained rank errors.

The 16 inventories expose active `ibp0`–`ibp7` InfiniBand ports and `mlx5_0`–`mlx5_8` Ethernet ports. NCCL 2.32.6 selected both. Local GPU 4 on every host (global ranks 4, 12, …, 124) reported `IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR(12)` on Ethernet HCAs, with vendor error 129; one also reported `IBV_WC_WR_FLUSH_ERR(5)`. All 128 workers subsequently aborted and all 16 durable gate reports failed. This pattern does not isolate one defective host.

Expected: the child request selects the InfiniBand rails before both the gate and serving start. Keep explicit runtime settings authoritative and keep the gate strict.

#11749 already sets `NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp` in the canonical cluster configuration, but that selection was absent from this task's effective NCCL device selection. The SkyRL launcher currently supplies only an rno2a bootstrap default, so this job depended on deployment-time environment delivery. The proposed fix sends the existing `ibp` choice explicitly in east02a child requests. A child-request regression fails on the original source and passes with the fix; live qualification remains pending.

Related: #11618 and #11749.

Relevant code: [child request construction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L1061-L1081), [east02a HCA config](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/config/cw-us-east-02a.yaml#L176-L181), [launcher task environment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/iris_backend.py#L882-L886).

## Proposed Fix

Set `NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp` in east02a child requests when `extra_env` does not specify it. Keep explicit recipe values authoritative and add a child-request regression covering the default and override.

issues.author: chrismc91
issues.body:
Curated evals give a judge-graded attempt enough grading time for one judge call. `grading_limits` (`lib/marin/src/marin/rollouts/evaluation.py:88`, added in #11967) extends the run's grading deadline to `max(transport_budget, request_timeout) + 30` s, the length of one judge transport window. Graders that make several judge calls per grade can still be cut off:

- FACTS Grounding's script grader calls the judge three times and declares `timeout = 60 + 3 * 1200 = 3660` s (`lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/facts_grounding.py:73`), but grading stops at 1230 s.
- verifyit's pairwise rubric judges both answer orders, and `incomplete_retry_tokens` makes a second request with a larger budget. Each call opens a new transport window.

Before #11967 every grader got a flat 600 s, so these deadlines are no shorter than they were. This came up in the review of #11967 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11967#issuecomment-7108487465)).

Done when:
- The grading deadline of a judged attempt comes from the grader: `ScriptGrader.timeout` for script graders, and a deadline exported by verifyit for verifyit judges that counts every call its rubric makes.
- verifyit holds the only copy of the per-call transport formula.
- A test shows a three-call judge grader gets its declared grading time.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

In #11967, `grading_limits` reserves one transport window plus 30 s for every judged task and ignores `ScriptGrader.timeout`. FACTS Grounding declares 3660 s but receives 1230 s. Verifyit's pairwise and checklist rubrics can make several requests; incomplete replies and rubric retries add more. No open PR targets #12150, and its deadline code is still in #11967.

**Relevant code**
- [`evaluation.py#L88-L98`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/69520b5686c38aa2d13894aae67d8e6299659ef0/lib/marin/src/marin/rollouts/evaluation.py#L88-L98) — one-window deadline
- [`facts_grounding.py#L68-L74`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/69520b5686c38aa2d13894aae67d8e6299659ef0/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/facts_grounding.py#L68-L74) — declared script timeout
- [`grade_judge.py#L520-L565`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/69520b5686c38aa2d13894aae67d8e6299659ef0/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L520-L565) — completion retry and pairwise calls
- [`grade_judge.py#L887-L944`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/69520b5686c38aa2d13894aae67d8e6299659ef0/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L887-L944) — checklist and score retry
- [`grade_judge.py#L751-L761`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/69520b5686c38aa2d13894aae67d8e6299659ef0/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L751-L761) — transport window

# Proposed Fix

1. Stack the change on #11967. For a judged script grader, use `ScriptGrader.timeout` as its grading deadline. For a verifyit judge, use a public verifyit function that returns the worst-case grade duration. Increase `attempt_timeout` by the same positive extension and preserve unlimited deadlines.
2. Keep the per-call transport window in verifyit and derive the full bound from each rubric's possible calls: both pairwise orders, each nonempty checklist criterion, incomplete-completion retries, and `_ask` score retries. Account for the OpenAI SDK retries in the reference/checklist path, or route those calls through verifyit's bounded transport path. Add the existing 30 s margin once per grade.
3. Add a failing regression showing FACTS Grounding receives its declared 3660 s, plus tests for pairwise incomplete-reply retries and checklist call accounting. Run the affected package tests, repository lint, and lint review; open a stacked PR with `Fixes #12150`. #10246 separately tracks cancellation of a synchronous judge call after its caller's deadline.
