comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 A reward-floor check on the NuminaMath-LEAN training tasks from #11095, before the first Lean RL run. I rebuilt the 4,035 tasks with the recipe's own `row_contract` on main `2bf3f721c`, drew 1,000 at random and compiled fixed replies against each statement in the grader's proof-term form, with the grader image's Lean v4.34.1 and Mathlib `d13f23b`. 795 of the 1,000 were graded in the time I had (the first 300 in order, then a random part of the other 700); the shares weight the two parts by their size.

| Fixed reply | Tasks proved (95% interval) |
|---|---|
| `grind` | 19% (16.5-22%) |
| `first \| (rfl; done) \| (decide; done) \| ... \| (exact?; done)` over 15 tactics | 25% (22-28%) |
| any one of `simp`, `norm_num`, `decide`, `omega`, `linarith`, `exact?`, `aesop`, `trivial`, `rfl` | 17% (14-19%) |

So about 1,000 of the 4,035 tasks give reward 1 to one constant reply. On ProofNet-Verified, `simp`, `simp_all`, `aesop`, `grind`, `tauto`, `ring` and `exact?` proved 49 of 366 rows through the grader (13%, in my #10879 review); those seven prove 24% here. Every task has a compiling human proof, so none is false, but in a random 200, `grind` derives `False` from the hypotheses of 4.

I read 20 of the proved tasks. 16 are faithful but easy: final computations such as `algebra_15505` (`gcd 2835 8960 = 35`), and answers that follow from the stated equations. 4 state less than their problem:

- `algebra_13062` (`fbf349fa`): `h : ∀ x, x ≠ 3 ∧ x ≠ -5 ∧ ...` is false at `x = 3`.
- `algebra_160868` (`ec81e530`): `∀ n, F n = F (n - 1) + F (n - 2)` over ℕ forces `F 0 = 0`, but `F 0 = 1`.
- `algebra_235251` (`f7637b05`): the equation that solves the frog problem is a hypothesis.
- `Number_Theory_640629` (`ed0dad30`): the egg problem became a statement whose inner condition cannot hold, so it is true for every `m`.

Two more have contradictory hypotheses: `algebra_174839` (`c1528388`) and `combinatorics_609372` (`3962696e`, `r = 50`, `b = 50`, `r - b = 5`).

A group in which every sample succeeds has no advantage, so most of these tasks only cost rollouts, and the vacuous ones reward a reply that ignores the problem. Grading the `first | ...` reply once per task at curation takes about 4 s a task in a batch. Would a filter, or a difficulty tag for the curriculum, be useful? I can add either to the recipe.

comments.author: Robertboy18
comments.body:
Thanks Xiaoyuan, this is really useful! Yes please, I think both would help:
- Drop the tasks whose hypotheses already prove `False` (your `grind` check), since any reply gets reward there.
- Tag the rest by whether the fixed `first | ...` reply proves them, so the selection recipe can drop or downweight the easy ones. Small models may still learn from them, so a tag seems better than a hard filter.

The ones that state less than the problem, like `algebra_235251` and `Number_Theory_640629`, won't show up in either check. On #11526 we ran the human problem text through a judge against the Lean for every row, and it caught a lot of these, so I'm happy to run the same thing over the 4,035 and send you the list :)

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body: Thanks Robert, will do. I'll open a PR that adds both to the NuminaMath-LEAN recipe: tasks where `grind` derives `False` from the hypotheses are dropped, and every other task is tagged with whether the fixed `first | ...` reply proves it, so the selection recipe can drop or downweight the easy ones. Your judge list would be great, since neither check sees the statements that say less than their problem; I'm happy to fold it in once you have it.

spillover_issues.title: [Data][RL] Marin needs high-quality Lean RL Data and better Lean Evals

spillover_issues.author: gonzalobenegas
spillover_issues.body:
## What

Add SWE-bench Science’s 96 unrestricted repository-repair tasks to Marin’s curated agentic evaluations. Mini-swe-agent works in the solver repository. The release’s collection hook exports the patch to a fresh verifier image, which rebuilds the software and runs the private tests. Each task earns 1 when all applicable private tests pass and 0 otherwise. [Pinned task selection](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/selections/default-96.json) · [Draft implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12109)

## Why

A scientific-code repair has to preserve the behavior checked by the repository’s private tests. This benchmark lets Marin compare models on that end-to-end task with the same harness, repositories, and grading rule. [Upstream benchmark](https://swescience.github.io/)

## Validation evidence

The release manifest, catalog selection, and paired results agree on all 96 task IDs. The initial conversion check found byte-identical instructions, matching image digests for all 96 solver/verifier pairs, and unchanged native timeouts. The release contains a further 23 tasks that require a restricted-license opt-in. [Pinned source and image declarations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/tree/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/tasks)

The two completed runs used mini-swe-agent with a 32,768-token context and an 8,192-token reply cap. Each model received one native grade per task.

| Model | Graded | Solved | Pass@1 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 96/96 | 5 | 5.21% |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B | 96/96 | 7 | 7.29% |

Both validation runs used Daytona for solver and verifier with 2 CPUs, 8 GiB RAM, and 10 GiB disk per sandbox. The release requests 20 GiB disk. The catalog uses the validated 10 GiB solver allocation and runs the verifier on its evaluator worker. Upstream’s leaderboard covers 119 tasks and uses several harnesses, which limits direct score comparisons. [Leaderboard](https://swescience.github.io/)

**Published reference target.** Table 2 of the original paper reports 42.02% on 119 tasks for DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 with Claude Code at max reasoning. A later leaderboard snapshot reports 39.50% for that model family. Filtering the snapshot’s per-task grades to the 96 IDs above gives 38/96 (39.58%). Use the pinned matrix for comparisons on the 96-task selection. [Paper, Table 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.19799v1#page=9) · [Pinned task matrix](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

The full runs used the development adapter. On review head `1d1c12efc6`, focused tests cover the 10 GiB solver request, nested package selection, patch collection, verifier image references, and reward parsing. #12109 is stacked on #11664 and registers the benchmark for explicit selection. Default-suite adoption is a separate decision. [Focused regression results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12109#issuecomment-7104344017) · [CI checks](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12109/checks)


**Same-patch replay.** On task 009, Marin and the standalone upstream Pier 0.3.0 runner each collected a patch with SHA-256 `b3ddf0be168d420135072fb14b06b8363e7feff7285a14fd7b39cfcb929d435b`. Both returned reward 1, with 1/1 public and 9/9 private tests passing. The patch was reconstructed from the Qwen3.6 cohort trajectory. The empty-patch control on the same task also matched across runners, with 0/1 public tests, 5/9 private tests, and reward 0. [Pinned upstream runner](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/scripts/run_batch.py)

**Same-patch replay on 17 Qwen3.8-27B tasks.** We froze the first graded patch available for each of 17 distinct tasks and replayed it through Marin without model calls. On all 17, Marin collected the same patch bytes (SHA-256) and reproduced the standalone Pier public and private test reports and reward. Both verifiers scored 7 solved and 10 unsolved. On these same IDs, the authors’ independent model run solved 9. The outcomes agreed on 15/17 IDs. Only 004 and 007 differed: the authors solved both, while our patches passed 0/15 and 5/6 private tests respectively under both verifiers. This establishes verifier agreement on the frozen sample. The sample was selected by archive availability and does not estimate full-benchmark model performance. [Published task matrix](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

**Matched Qwen3.8-27B harness comparison.** Marin ran Pi 0.87.0 and Mini-SWE-Agent 2.1.0 with the same checkpoint (`37561816e66b5b9153b1b64c10968c18c1e6f4a0`), 32,768-token context, 8,192-token reply limit, explicit `xhigh`, and native task verifiers. We selected six tasks from existing Pi and Claude Code grades before running Mini-SWE-Agent. The full Pi run stopped with 100 graded and 3 solved.

| Task IDs | Marin Pi | Marin Mini-SWE-Agent | Upstream Pier + Claude Code (our run) | Authors’ Claude Code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 001, 003 | Neither solved | Neither solved | Neither solved | Neither solved |
| 012, 015 | Neither solved | Neither solved | Both solved | Both solved |
| 013, 028 | Both solved | Neither solved | Both solved | Both solved |
| Solved | 2/6 | 0/6 | 4/6 | 4/6 |

Mini-SWE-Agent hit the context ceiling on 001 and 028. Its final replies had only 24 and 43 tokens available respectively. On 012 and 015, both Marin harnesses passed 5/10 and 17/31 private tests respectively. The panel was selected by previous outcomes, so its solve rates apply only to these six tasks. The Claude Code comparison also changes inference provider. [Authors’ task matrix](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

**Task 028 context-window check.** With Qwen3.8-27B, Mini-SWE-Agent 2.1.0, explicit `xhigh`, and an 8,192-token per-reply cap, increasing the context window from 32,768 to 65,536 changed the native grade from 0 to 1. At 32k, the last seven replies stopped for length without a tool call. The final prompt left 43 tokens for the reply; the patch passed 0/1 public and 2/10 private tests. At 65k, the agent tested its changes and explicitly submitted on turn 29 with a 51,151-token prompt. It passed 1/1 public and 10/10 private tests. Pi 0.87.0 passed all tests at 32k after summarizing its history twice. This was one fresh attempt at each setting on a task selected for a context-limit failure. The six-task results above retain their original settings and scores.

**Reference-model pilot.** Qwen3.8-27B with Claude Code 2.1.330 at xhigh solved unrestricted task 013. The standalone Pier verifier returned 1/1 public tests, 5/5 private tests, and reward 1, matching the authors’ task 013 result. On the same task, Qwen3.5-9B at max passed 1/1 public and 3/5 private tests, earning reward 0. The pinned task matrix has no per-task 9B reference. These pilot grades cover one task per model. The authors solved 29 of the same 96 unrestricted tasks. [Authors’ task 013 trace](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-013.json)

<details>
<summary>License decision for the 96-task and 119-task selections</summary>

Keep the upstream **default 96** as the named comparison set for the runs reported here. The adapter should also support an explicit **full 119** selection so we can compare with the published leaderboard. The draft currently selects 96. Report the selection and graded count alongside each score. [Upstream selection policy](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/README.md#restricted-licenses)

- **18 copyleft tasks.** GPL, LGPL, or AGPL status alone is insufficient reason to exclude a task from evaluation or numerical score reporting. Check the applicable terms for hosted execution and for any distribution of images, source, or patches.
- **019, 026, 101 — terms affecting use.** Confirm that Marin’s research use and hosted processing are covered. For 019, the pinned pycisTopic repository contains an internal-academic-use license that names SCENIC+, limits copying outside the laboratory, and requests acknowledgment in manuscripts. Its scope needs clarification. For 026 the flag concerns bundled academic non-commercial material. For 101 it concerns parameter files derived from a CC BY-NC-ND article. Keeping traces private still leaves the copies made during execution to consider. [Pinned pycisTopic license](https://github.com/aertslab/pycisTopic/blob/cb5f54111d2affd89ad732c20c14dab6138026f0/LICENSE.txt) · [CC BY-NC-ND terms](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/legalcode.en#s2a)
- **035, 102 — redistribution questions.** Upstream flags the NASA ODEPACK report in 035 and force-field records in 102. Publishing a numerical score does not reproduce those files. For the hosted run, check which materials the sandbox and inference provider receive. Review any later release of images, patches, or traces containing source or materials separately. [Per-task notices](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/data/tasks.csv)

**27B run selection, 23 November.** The current run targets 114 tasks: the upstream default 96 plus the 18 GPL-family tasks listed below. The 18 are approved for the current hosted scoring workflow with upstream notices preserved. Tasks 019, 026, 035, 101 and 102 remain pending individual permission decisions. Report the scored denominator explicitly when comparing with the authors’ 119-task result. Public release of source-bearing traces is a separate decision.

**Hosted-run review, 23 November.** These are the execution decisions for the 23 opt-in IDs. Numerical scores can be reported separately from any release of patches, source, or trajectories.

| Task IDs | Disposition and reason |
| --- | --- |
| 003, 020, 021, 032, 057, 066, 074, 075, 082, 083, 084, 085, 096, 097, 098, 118 | **Included in the 114-task hosted run.** The pinned source and task notices identify GPL/LGPL components. Preserve the notices in the images and any applicable attribution. Task 032 includes LGPL-covered OpenMM platform code. Task 074 excludes the cited NC-ND paper. Private execution and a numeric score present no identified copyleft-specific obstacle. The opt-in covers the benchmark run and numerical results. |
| 023 | **Same execution recommendation.** The release flags AGPL; the [pinned MDAnalysis license](https://github.com/MDAnalysis/mdanalysis/blob/2acd594449c02c2a354b07291031d89b50b52186/LICENSE) describes a GPLv3-or-later combination with component exceptions. Preserve that discrepancy in the record. The solver runs the program in an isolated workspace. Offering a modified program as a network service would warrant separate review. |
| 100 | **Same execution recommendation for the pinned snapshot.** Upstream records conflicting MIT/LGPL declarations. The [pinned license file](https://github.com/DCoupry/autografs/blob/c2f22341f2b1eb2f619b76534cf4abe2e5e6b3a3/LICENSE.txt) specifies LGPL. Preserve the mixed notices and avoid describing the whole snapshot as MIT. |
| 019 | **Permission unresolved.** The solver image copies the repository. The pinned academic license limits who may use and copy the software, and names SCENIC+ in the pycisTopic repository. Confirm applicability, institutional eligibility, and coverage of hosted copies or obtain permission. |
| 026 | **Permission unresolved.** The flag concerns the [WRF technical note](https://www2.mmm.ucar.edu/wrf/users/docs/technote/v4_technote.pdf). MetPy itself is BSD. The solver recipe copies the public assets, but the exact bundled document was not independently verified against the image. Check the edition, its grant, and whether the evaluation qualifies. |
| 035 | **Permission unresolved for hosted copies.** The [materials manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/tasks/task_035/environment/public/MATERIALS.json) places the NASA report PDF and extracted text in the solver’s public assets. Verify the rights for this report or obtain permission for these copies. |
| 101 | **Permission unresolved.** The [required Chen2020 CSVs](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/tasks/task_101/environment/public/MATERIALS.json) are in the solver source tree. Confirm the non-commercial purpose and coverage for the hosted workflow. Removing the parameters would change the benchmark. |
| 102 | **Permission unresolved for hosted copies.** The [2016H66 force-field records](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/tasks/task_102/environment/public/MATERIALS.json) are in the solver source tree. The release could not establish a complete per-file redistribution grant. Verify that the intended recipients are covered. |

**Why the inference arrangement matters.** Daytona’s public terms limit its customer-content license to providing the service. OpenRouter’s public terms (§§6.1, 6.5–6.6) cover service operations and anonymized metrics, include sublicensing rights, and ask the submitter to have the necessary permissions. The 27B route pins Chutes with no fallback and does not explicitly request zero retention. At review time the exact model/provider pair did not appear in OpenRouter’s public zero-retention list. Actual account-level settings and any negotiated agreement remain unverified. Private execution with source-bearing prompts sent to a provider and publication of a numerical score are distinct uses. This review does not establish that GPL-family licenses prohibit hosted inference. [Daytona terms](https://www.daytona.io/terms-of-service) · [OpenRouter terms](https://openrouter.ai/terms) · [Provider retention policy](https://www.chutes.ai/privacy) · [OpenRouter zero-retention endpoints](https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr) · [Pinned task manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/data/tasks.csv)

</details>

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

PR #11664 is the prerequisite for this catalog entry and remains open. Its curated Harbor path already has mini-swe-agent and separate verifier machines, but the package stager scans only top-level Hugging Face directories and the importer rejects task schema 1.3. The SWE-bench Science release places tasks under `tasks/task_###`, selects 96 unrestricted tasks, and uses `pre_artifacts.sh` to produce the candidate patch; the current importer does not run that hook.

**Relevant code**
- [#11664 `agentic.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/experiments/evaluation/benchmarks/agentic.py#L296-L355): mini-swe-agent catalog pattern.
- [#11664 `harbor_packages.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/experiments/post_training/task_curation/harbor_packages.py#L50-L60): top-level package discovery.
- [#11664 `config.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/harbor/config.py#L18): supported schemas.
- [#11664 `package.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/harbor/package.py#L327-L355): separate grading and collect hooks.
- [Release task 002](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/SWE-bench-Science/blob/main/huggingface/tasks/task_002/pre_artifacts.sh): patch collection contract.

# Proposed Fix

1. Build on #11664 after it lands. Pin `OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science@997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb`; read its selection manifest and require exactly the 96 unrestricted task IDs. Check the pinned snapshot's layout and image references before importing.
2. Extend package staging for the nested task directory and schema 1.3. Preserve each original `instruction.md`, timeout, CPU, memory, storage, and image digest. Run the release's patch-collection hook after mini-swe-agent exits, transfer `model.patch` to a fresh digest-pinned verifier machine, and keep private tests there.
3. Register a `swebench-science` catalog key and image lock using the existing mini-swe-agent protocol. Add it to the agentic suite after the smoke confirms that the selected resource and concurrency settings work.
4. Test selection, schema parsing, patch handoff, and verifier reward collection with small synthetic packages. Run the upstream no-model verifier smoke, then a served mini-swe-agent smoke and a full 96-task run; compare a sample patch's score with the upstream runner.
5. Publish the source pin, selected IDs, harness revision, environment and verifier digests, resource limits, concurrency, per-task scoring coverage, failure classes, and aggregate Pass@1 with the run artifacts. Complete the entry when all 96 tasks have a verifier result or a reported infrastructure failure.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 The issue body now records the validation evidence for this proposal. The catalog’s 96 IDs match the pinned selection manifest exactly. #12109 handles the nested packages and Pier 1.3 collection hook, preserves the upstream image digests and deadlines, and grades the patch in a separate verifier. Both model cohorts finished with 96/96 grades.

The draft is stacked on #11664 while it is under review. The source task manifests already pin both images, so they serve as the image lock. The catalog uses the validated 10 GiB solver allocation and leaves default-suite inclusion for a policy decision. The empty-patch control exercised the release’s native verifier. Independent scoring of the same saved patch through the standalone upstream runner is still open.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 On the 100 graded Qwen3.8-27B tasks, Pi 0.87.0 solved 3 and the authors’ Claude Code run solved 31 on the same IDs. All three Pi solves were also solved upstream. These 100 are the graded portion of an interrupted run.

I classified the last recorded model request by its system prompt and finish reason. In **75/100** trajectories, the last request was a compaction summary that reached its output limit. Of those, 74 ended at exactly 6,553 completion tokens and one at 4,096. This includes **21 of the 28** tasks solved only by the authors. It establishes a recurring failure mode. The number of solves recoverable by changing the limits is still open. [Authors’ per-task grades](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

Pi budgets a main summary at 80% of the reserved output tokens, rounded down, and a split-turn prefix at 50%. With an 8,192-token reserve those limits are 6,553 and 4,096. Pi rejects a summary whose provider stop reason is length, including summaries containing partial text. The older Harbor investigation found a separate Terminus-2 fallback that could omit the latest tool observation. Its larger-budget follow-up also showed why completed handoffs, resumed solver steps and grades should be measured separately. [Pi 0.87.0 compaction implementation](https://unpkg.com/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@0.87.0/dist/core/compaction/compaction.js) · [Harbor #165](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/165)

Two matched controls use tasks 012 and 015 at 65,536 context with explicit xhigh, at 8,192 and 16,384 reply tokens. Both tasks have public successful reference traces. The authors report 40,670 output tokens across 21 calls on 012 and 420,892 across 60 calls on 015. Their published aggregates do not give a per-call maximum. [Task 012](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-012.json) · [Task 015](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-015.json)

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 All four matched Pi attempts graded. At a 65,536-token context, doubling the per-reply limit recovered the authors’ task 012 solve. Task 015 still failed. This is one attempt per condition on two selected disagreements.

| Task | 32,768 context / 8,192 reply | 65,536 / 8,192 | 65,536 / 16,384 | Authors’ Claude Code |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 012 private tests | 5/10 | 5/10 | **10/10** | 10/10 |
| 015 private tests | 17/31 | 17/31 | 17/31 | 31/31 |

All four new attempts passed their public test. The checkpoint, Pi 0.87.0, xhigh, tasks and verifiers were held fixed. Both model-request receipts confirmed the intended reply cap and enabled thinking.

**012.** Neither 65,536-context attempt compacted. After normalizing generated tool-call IDs, the archived input messages matched on calls 1 through 9. On call 9 both had 19,407 prompt tokens. At the smaller cap the model used 8,192 tokens and returned no visible text or tool call. At the larger cap it used 15,364 tokens, requested two tools, and issued two edits on the next call. The native grade rose from zero to one. [Authors’ task 012 trace](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-012.json)

**015.** Increasing the reply limit also increased Pi’s compaction reserve, which changed when it summarized and how much recent history it kept. At the smaller cap, one of five summary calls finished normally. At the larger cap, four of nine did and coding resumed after each. The final summary still hit its limit of 13,107 tokens. Summaries used 90,981 of the 167,081 generated tokens in the larger-budget trace (54%). Passing more handoffs did not improve the native grade. The authors report 420,892 generated tokens across 60 calls on this task. [Authors’ task 015 trace](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-015.json)

**Frozen-summary replay on 015.** I replayed the final 21,393-token input on the same checkpoint at xhigh, with a fixed seed (42) shared across two output caps. Both replies stopped normally after 11,351 output tokens, at caps of 13,107 and 26,214. Both produced visible text with goal, progress, next steps and critical context headings. The archived live call had hit the 13,107 cap. This single replay shows that this input can finish within the existing limit and that another sample can behave differently. It did not resume the solver or produce a task grade. No content-quality score was assigned to the summaries.

RL consumes exactly 32 SWE + 32 non-agentic groups per update, eight samples per group (512 trajectories), with maximum staleness of two optimizer updates. Its explicit budget is 10 h from the first completed optimizer step, with a 1,800-second drain margin. Validation and native saves occur every two updates. Selection uses an EMA with span five (alpha 1/3) and requires all 120 validation tasks scored; selected step 20 scored 120/120. Retention is last three plus protected best.   --validation-output experiments/post_training/long_loop/runtime-inputs/20261114-exp2-recovery13/validation \

Reproduction requires fresh output versions, the frozen inputs, Marin storage access and configured secret bindings (`HF_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY`, `CW_KEY_ID`/`CW_KEY_SECRET`, `DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY`, `DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY`, `DAYTONA_TARGET=us`, `TOGETHER_API_KEY`). ## 10/05 Micro210 baseline

Evaluation-only entry for the frozen 10/05 model; this does not introduce a new SFT or RL training recipe.

Micro210 is Marin’s mixed reasoning, knowledge, coding and agentic evaluation suite.
This recipe supports 200 distinct tasks across 20 sources (Tau3 excluded), expanded to 440 assignments, including 100 Pi assignments.

## Model and evaluation policy

Model: [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05/tree/ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6), immutable revision `ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6`. The three runs evaluate this same model in existing region-local storage, with no additional training.

The runtime separately selects [marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools](https://huggingface.co/marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools/tree/3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09), revision `3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09`, with no explicit template override and thinking enabled. The model’s embedded tokenizer provenance is not the selected runtime tools revision.

Current harness: 16 global Harbor slots (four rollout workers × four), one 8 H100 policy worker (TP1/DP8/EP8, max_num_seqs 8) and an independent 8 H100 M3 judge (TP8). Policy/judge caps are 21,600 s; root cap is 25,200 s. Native Pi 0.87; context 65,536, 16,384 generated tokens per turn, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95. Compilation and CUDA graphs remain enabled. These role budgets are not asserted identical to every historical recipe in this issue.

Pinned policy image request: `13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8`. The region-control policy image matched that request; its CPU/judge/broker task image was `b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`, matching the observed cw-us-east-02a reference. Policy/judge runtime pins are `39e62869693c` / `01911be34fac`; judge model revision is `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Images and pins do not independently attest imported module bytes or platform equivalence.

All three produced suite Parquets are 16,401,114 bytes with SHA256 `00cdda0654be66060d3ff77b6b44e3dc6fa470e50625ef61ef24b5d9c778bef7`. Produced-byte/order identity is not live runtime consumption or complete assigned-UID coverage proof.

## Scores and coverage

Native equal-20 is recomputed from the 20 native source averages, whose denominators include excluded assignments. Available-only means omit excluded outcomes. Scores are heterogeneous partial-credit means, not pass@1.

| Run 2 (44628) | cw-us-east-02a | 47.32% | 47.42% | 40.91% | 433 / 440 | 7 | 5 | 28.43 |
| Region control (44633) | cw-rno2a | 47.98% | 48.44% | 40.31% | 436 / 440 | 4 | 7* | 26.04 |

Run 2 has one BixBench and six TB2 unknowns. The region control has one BFCL, one BixBench and two TB2 unknowns. Its BFCL slice has seven known score units from nine scored assignments plus one unknown, giving assigned-score bounds 7–8/10. Unknown outcomes are not known zero or failure.

The two cw-us-east-02a runs differ by 5.22 task-equivalents (run 2 minus run 1: -5.218662810; unknown-outcome bounds [-5.218662810, +1.781337190]). This is one observed same-configuration evaluation repeat difference of about five tasks, not a calibrated eval-noise estimate, universal tie band, confidence interval or independent training-seed replication. These are fractional assignment-weighted score masses, not integer additional wins or matched individual outcomes. The RNO control is descriptive; it does not isolate a causal region effect.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 On Canonical Micro210, a constant reply scores above Round 3 on TruthfulQA and GPQA Diamond, and 40% on MMLU-Pro. I graded the 140 prepared answer-only tasks, rebuilt with #11120's `prepare_micro` (sha256 equal to `prepared_rollouts_sha256` in #11686), with Round 3's tokenizer, context and output limits. The five replies of the `trivial_replies` launcher in the open #11222 (empty, `hello`, `0`, `I don't know.`, the prompt repeated) went through `run_evaluation`. Single letters went through the rows' own rollout specs.

| Benchmark | Constant reply | Score (%) | Round 1 | Round 2 | Round 3 | Base | Snowball v0.1 |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TruthfulQA | `\boxed{A}` | 100 | 70 | 80 | 70 | 20 | 90 |
| GPQA Diamond | `B` | 50 | 56.7 | 56.7 | 43.3 | 33.3 | 66.7 |
| MMLU-Pro | `I don't know.` | 40 | 70 | 70 | 60 | 40 | 90 |
| IFBench | `hello` | 10 | 40 | 40 | 30 | 0 | 40 |

The other ten answer benchmarks score 0 for every reply. The six agentic benchmarks were not run.

- TruthfulQA: the generated-choice prompts list the options in `mc2_targets` order, which starts with a true answer. Option A is true in every task: 10 in Micro210, 41 in Mini840, 817 rows of `truthfulqa/truthful_qa`. A seeded shuffle of each task's options would remove this. The full policy's MC2 likelihood scoring does not depend on order.
- MMLU-Pro: without `answer is (X)` or `Answer: X`, the extractor takes the last standalone capital A-J, so `I don't know.` counts as option I, the key of 4 tasks.
- GPQA Diamond: 5 of the 10 drawn keys are B.
- IFBench: the prepared rows grade it with the `evalchemy` wheel of `runtime-v4`, whose IFBench checkers are byte-identical to `vendor/evalchemy` before #10423. In one of the 10 tasks (key 278, the capitals of European countries north of 45°) a correct reply cannot pass: the checker's list leaves out Kyiv, so the 28 correct capitals score 0 and the 27 without Kyiv score 1.

This does not show that a round guesses. On these 10 tasks, the three benchmarks cannot tell a round from a constant below the floor. They carry 8.7 of Round 3's 41.07 points. Without them, Rounds 1-3, the base and Snowball v0.1 average 49.8, 44.7, 38.1, 13.3 and 40.3%.

Launcher floors rerun with `trivial_replies` on #11222's head over a TaskSpec corpus of a benchmark's prepared tasks. The TruthfulQA count needs only the dataset (`uv run --with pyarrow --with huggingface_hub python check.py`):

```python
import base64, json
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

path = hf_hub_download("open-athena/Marin-Micro-Eval-210", "data/validation.parquet", repo_type="dataset",
                       revision="4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819")
labels = []
for row in pq.read_table(path).to_pylist():
    if row["benchmark"] == "truthfulqa":
        files = json.loads(row["task_spec"])["resources"]["verifier"]
        config = json.loads(base64.b64decode(next(f for f in files if f["path"] == "config.json")["source"]["content_base64"]))
        labels.append(config["spec"]["doc"]["mc2_targets"]["labels"][0])
print(f"option A is true in {sum(labels)} of {len(labels)} TruthfulQA tasks")
```

The uncertainty calculation follows the prior Exp3 seal and [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Each benchmark uses the conservative task-level SEM bound `s = 0.5/sqrt(10*0.9)`, including the 90% valid-trial allowance. With scored fractions `r_b`, means `m_b` and weights `w_b=1/20`, set `mu=sum(w_b*r_b*m_b)`, `delta=sum(w_b*(1-r_b))` and `sigma=sqrt(sum((w_b*r_b*s)^2))`. The Imbens–Manski critical value solves `Phi(c+delta/sigma)-Phi(-c)=0.95`; here `c=1.9381`. The interval is `[mu-c*sigma, mu+c*sigma+delta]`, clipped to [0,1]; benchmark intervals use one cell. ### Coverage, errors and audit

All 440 frozen attempt IDs occur exactly once. Reporting retains 418 scoreable attempts across 18 cells; this includes the ten verifier-completed but uninformative TruthfulQA attempts. Removing TruthfulQA leaves 408/430 scoreable attempts (94.88%) across 19 informative declared benchmarks, of which 17 have scores. The remaining 22 trials are absent; no missing reward is imputed.

- **BixBench: 0/10.** Nine verifier `ValueError` exceptions state: `Provider credentials must remain on the host; use a Shellbox model relay: OPENAI_API_KEY` ([#12094](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12094)). One sandbox creation returned `DaytonaError:502 Bad Gateway`. None has a verifier grade.
- **Terminal-Bench 2: 28/30 (93.33%).** Two `VerifierTimeoutError` trials on `mcmc-sampling-stan` reached the frozen 300 s verifier limit. Both are absent.
- **CRUXEval: N/A.** All ten zero-score traces were reviewed through the frozen input program, model assertion, parsing and retained verifier diagnostics. Nine output literals are correct; five of those also use the requested answer tags. All ten verifier processes exited 0 and printed 0.0. The zero does not pass the trace audit. The frozen cell is rejected under [#11922](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11922), as in the SFT baseline. No semantic replacement scores are assigned. These receipts do not establish the exact subprocess mechanism for each zero.
- **TruthfulQA: uninformative.** All ten prepared rows put a true answer at option A ([#12060](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12060)). Its observed value enters no capability mean. In fixed-panel bounds only, the cell is unknown in [0, 1].

The ten Harbor `AgentTimeoutError` trials retain six verifier zeros and four verifier ones. The 24 `ContextLengthExceededError` trials retain 19 zeros and five ones, under #10197’s Harbor rule. All other unnamed or infrastructure-classified failures remain absent. Native rows and policy bytes are unchanged.

Approximate intervals use the [existing `evalrecords` Imbens–Manski bounded-missing-panel implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c751a4907dc7d2053c85b13c7ce57dab9c7737bf/lib/evalrecords/src/evalrecords/eval_stats.py), with an independent-task normal approximation. Each benchmark uses a conservative task-level standard-error bound `0.5/sqrt(10*0.9)`, which includes the policy’s 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. Repeated trials are not independent tasks. Unknown cells and absent trials are bounded in [0, 1]. The informative attempt-weighted 95% interval is **29.27%–57.82%**. With ten tasks per benchmark, these are descriptive approximations, not exact finite-sample coverage guarantees. They exclude serving-stack reproducibility.

### Model, recipe and evidence

- Model: [open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round5-2026.11.23.140-step22 @ `32a2c26a`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round5-2026.11.23.140-step22/tree/32a2c26a1e9868eb52bc49d1b5c0e6424785664e). The permanent native final remains protected.
- SFT: V7 on 256 H100; final native step 527. Curriculum `long-loop/exp5-rl@2026.11.20:995e3844` draws 13/51 agentic/nonagentic groups with a disjoint 200-prompt holdout. [Exact consumed launch](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Flong-loop-exp5%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fcheckpoints%2Fmochi-exp5-rl%2F2026.11.23.140%2Fresolved-launch.yaml). spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Some RL sources call live third-party services from their tasks, and Atlas has no design for giving those tasks credentials. Such sources are excluded with `ExclusionReason.THIRD_PARTY_CREDENTIALS_REQUIRED` until a design exists.

The first example is MCP-Atlas (`ScaleAI/mcp-atlas`, with the native harness `scaleapi/mcp-atlas`). Its 500-row parent set runs live MCP servers that need 21 credentials: `AIRTABLE_API_KEY`, `ALCHEMY_API_KEY`, `BRAVE_API_KEY`, `E2B_API_KEY`, `EXA_API_KEY`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_REFRESH_TOKEN`, `LARA_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `LARA_ACCESS_KEY_SECRET`, `MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING`, `NOTION_TOKEN`, `NPS_API_KEY`, `OXYLABS_USERNAME`, `OXYLABS_PASSWORD`, `SLACK_MCP_XOXC_TOKEN`, `SLACK_MCP_XOXD_TOKEN`, `TWELVE_DATA_API_KEY` and `WEATHER_API_KEY`. Four source tool prefixes are also missing from the pinned runtime template: `rijksmuseum-server`, `balldontlie`, `f1-mcp-server` and `anili`. The 220-row MCP-Atlas Easy set needs no live tools and is admitted separately.

Test or fixture accounts are acceptable in principle. Provisioning many of them needs a design first.

Done when a design is written and approved that covers:
- Which services are worth provisioning. Selection is by task count and eval value; alternatives are recorded tool fixtures or substitute servers.
- Account model: one test tenant per service, owned by the project, never a personal account, with no access to production data or real users.
- Scope: credentials bind only to the owned MCP service and verifier jobs, never to the agent's tool containers or sandbox environment, and only for the job that needs them.
- Storage and delivery through Iris secrets, with submission failing when a required secret is missing or empty.
- Rotation, revocation and leak response, including how credentials are kept out of logs and published artifacts.
- Cost and rate limits per service at expected rollout and eval volume.
- How a source declares its required credentials, so Atlas can type the exclusion and clear it once the qualifier passes with fixture credentials.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

MCP-Atlas's live parent set needs a service boundary before its credentials can be provisioned. On current `main`, curation's source declaration has no credential-requirement field and admission is projected from tags and pipeline availability; Iris can deliver isolated per-job secret files, but Shellbox's existing `secret_env` path resolves values into sandbox environment variables and is explicitly reserved for trusted private grading. That path cannot serve model-controlled MCP actors.

**Relevant code**
- [`source.py#L117-L193`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e1742c045d2ce976c6c8a78d1cf9beb439f054c3/experiments/post_training/task_curation/source.py#L117-L193) — source metadata contract.
- [`sources.py#L106-L114`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e1742c045d2ce976c6c8a78d1cf9beb439f054c3/experiments/post_training/task_curation/sources.py#L106-L114) — runnable-source gate.
- [`secrets.md#L1-L68`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e1742c045d2ce976c6c8a78d1cf9beb439f054c3/lib/iris/docs/secrets.md#L1-L68) — file delivery and isolation.
- [`machine.py#L305-L331`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e1742c045d2ce976c6c8a78d1cf9beb439f054c3/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py#L305-L331) and [`#L388-L404`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e1742c045d2ce976c6c8a78d1cf9beb439f054c3/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py#L388-L404) — grading-only secret path.

# Proposed Fix

This is a design task spanning source admission, Iris delivery, MCP execution, and service ownership. Write a one-page design and contract spec for review before provisioning accounts or admitting the live parent set:

1. Inventory the pinned 500 rows by MCP server, required credential set, task count, and eval value. Record one disposition per service: project-owned test tenant, recorded tool fixture or substitute server, or deferred. Include the four missing runtime tool prefixes. Keep the 220-row Easy set separate.
2. Define source-owned, typed credential requirements containing service IDs and secret names, never values. Specify how an unmet requirement yields `THIRD_PARTY_CREDENTIALS_REQUIRED` in the current catalog model, and require a passing fixture-backed qualifier before clearing that reason for an admitted subset.
3. Put each selected credential in a project-owned tenant with synthetic data and minimum service scope. Deliver it through Iris `EnvironmentSpec.secrets` to only the trusted MCP service and verifier jobs, with `SecretBehavior.ISOLATE`; reject missing or empty values before submission. Have a trusted orchestrator forward only declared tool calls to those services and return bounded results to the model. The agent sandbox receives no service credential, inherited secret, or service mount. Specify this connection path explicitly because Iris SANDBOX jobs cannot reach cluster services under their current egress policy.
4. Specify per-service request, concurrency, rate, and spend ceilings at expected rollout and eval volume; ownership of tenant creation, rotation and revocation; and leak response. Include redaction checks for Iris logs, curation evidence, and published artifacts, plus access controls and retention for controller persistence. Iris currently stores submitted secret values in its database and checkpoints, so that exposure must be part of the review.
5. Qualify one service end to end with a fixture tenant: missing/empty-secret rejection, successful tool and verifier calls, enforced limits, and canary checks that the actor container and published artifacts contain no key. Expand only to services whose accounts, limits, and native harness support pass the same checks; retain typed exclusions for the rest.

The design review must choose the first services and their budgets from the row inventory. #10486 and #10819 cover related agent and orchestrator credential boundaries; reuse those contracts where they apply. No live-source admission or account provisioning should precede that review.

spillover_issues.author: WhenWen
spillover_issues.body:
Prompted by Calvin Xu @Calvin-Xu 

Where would the final Mochi base model land on the base-model log-perplexity plot shared by Elie Bakouch? We can measure how well Mochi predicts public code and use open models that appear on the plot to estimate its position. The estimate inherits uncertainty because the public code and the plot use different evaluation data. [Original plot](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972) · [OpenAI evaluation](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/) · [Earlier Marin PPL comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8824)

### Estimated position on the original plot

![Elie Bakouch’s full comparison chart with the final Mochi estimate marked as an orange star.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/e5a6e3d019f9efd4cf8089daded2cbf45af3c179/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/mochi-final-placement.png)

Elie Bakouch’s original figure includes the OpenAI series, MAI-1 and MAI-2 Base, the green MAI-paper comparisons, and the purple Inkling comparisons with their calibration ranges. The orange star adds Mochi at its November 17 release date. Its height (0.879) comes from our separate July-code calibration using DeepSeek V4 Pro Base, Kimi K2 Base, and Gemma 4 31B. [Original figure and method by Elie Bakouch](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972)

### Direct measurement

Score the released **Mochi base checkpoint at step 393,491** and **Gemma 4 31B base** on the same 500 C++ files and 500 Python files from July 2026 UncheatableEval. Both Iris runs use 4,096-token windows and each model’s native tokenizer. For each language, sum the prediction loss across all tokens and divide by the total number of UTF-8 bytes. Report bits per byte (lower is better), then give the two languages equal weight in the comparison. [Pinned dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07/tree/65889535d56aa38d448ce7e07b08e6e36c031545) · [Mochi checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Marin-Mochi-535B-A23B/tree/c8bb74061a11f21bc4b432e498060e2cb199e40c) · [Gemma checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B/tree/5bbc2fb1c1b2c611d06e3d9f23c170ba21659d89)

### Results to record

- [x] Report direct C++ and Python bits per byte for both models.
- [x] Compare our Gemma scores with its published July results (0.25293 C++, 0.33209 Python) to quantify the effect of scoring settings.
- [x] Report the estimated Mochi plot coordinate with two anchors and with Gemma included. Show how much the choice changes the answer.

### Direct July results

Both Iris runs completed. Each row uses the same 500 C++ and 500 Python files at a 4,096-token scoring window. Lower bits per byte mean better prediction.

| Base model | C++ | Python | Mean of languages |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Mochi, final step 393,491 | 0.22355 | 0.29184 | 0.25769 |
| Gemma 4 31B | 0.25293 | 0.33205 | 0.29249 |

![Direct July C++ and Python bits per byte for Mochi and three open models. Mochi falls between DeepSeek V4 Pro Base and Kimi K2 Base on both.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/126400d006cf2d8e012ba2aa73647428f237d879/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/july-code-scores.png)

Mochi lands between DeepSeek V4 Pro Base and Kimi K2 Base in both languages. DeepSeek and Kimi use Marin’s archived July measurements.

The Gemma rerun is within 0.00005 bits/byte of the published score in each language. For Mochi, DeepSeek and Kimi give an estimated chart coordinate of **0.8788**. Including Gemma gives **0.8795**. When held out, Gemma's estimated chart height misses its inferred reference by **0.0103**. The two Mochi estimates agreeing within 0.0007 therefore understates the uncertainty in translating public code loss to OpenAI’s evaluation. [Public July data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07) · [Code-to-chart calibration sources](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/Frontier-Pre-training-at-Microsoft-AI.pdf)

### Contamination check

**Confirmed code-bearing overlap in 19 July files (10 C++, 9 Python).** The matching passages range from common scaffolding and generated code to a vendored TinyXML implementation. One 4,096-token training sequence at step 150,417 contains 1,174 consecutive tokens from the scored July file, including string encoding and XML node operations. The July repository reused code that Mochi had already seen. [Pinned July file](https://github.com/takagi-ryo-ac/RTSS/blob/86a93eaaeff19ccca78272a183028154536bea29/tinyxml.cpp)

| Example | Consecutive tokens in a single training sequence | Zero-based training step |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TinyXML library implementation, C++ | 1,174 of 2,518 scored tokens | 150,417 |
| Alembic online/offline migration template, Python | 278 of 546 | 220,782 |
| Qt-generated meta-object code, C++ | 167 of 1,152 | 150,985 |
| Dear ImGui Win32/OpenGL example, C++ | 91 of 2,017 | 177,190 |

**Audit method.** We sampled 15,872 distinct blocks from 16 code-heavy training-data buckets during steps 146,355–231,664. All 16,642,998,272 sampled tokens came from shuffle windows fully consumed by that run. We searched for 48-token exact matches, starting every 16 test tokens and requiring at least 12 identifier, operator or keyword positions outside strings and comments. We extended each match to its exact boundaries. For each of the 19 files, we replayed a witness through the pinned training loader and independently reread its bytes from the training store. Two Qt-generated files and one Alembic template account for 365 of the 404 match occurrences. A file can occur repeatedly. [Recorded training run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k) · [Pinned data loader](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ad754c6d67555d6369a4a312ff7388e43cfd08c1/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/dataset.py)

**Effect on the comparison.** Both models are rescored from their stored per-file losses on the same retained files. The gap is Gemma BPB minus Mochi BPB. Positive values favor Mochi.

| July files retained | C++ files | C++ gap | Python files | Python gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All | 500 | 0.02939 | 500 | 0.04021 |
| Exclude the 19 files with verified code overlap | 490 | 0.02923 | 491 | 0.03991 |
| Exclude entire files with obvious license or copyright markers | 465 | 0.02611 | 483 | 0.03981 |
| Exclude the union of those sets and earlier flagged files | 453 | 0.02536 | 473 | 0.03903 |

The 19 confirmed files establish a lower bound. Most training tokens were outside the scan, and edited copies can evade exact matching. The public-code comparison with Gemma survives every exclusion above. The 0.879 chart estimate still uses the full July data, since matching per-file scores for DeepSeek and Kimi are needed to recalibrate the filtered comparison.

#### Earlier license and training-pool checks


Marin's training-time decontamination corpus omitted UncheatableEval. The benchmark’s GitHub crawler filters by repository creation date, samples a file, and records the repository push date. Old code and licenses can occur in a new repository. [Marin decontamination audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10541) · [July crawler](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval/blob/bf068ff0863f1f3398b20a8ae64f50c29765e860/crawlers/crawler/spiders/github.py#L112)

A targeted scan of 201,326,592 tokens in the final run’s Harrier data store found exact passages in three July files. For two, I reconstructed the training batch with the recorded run configuration and the pinned Levanter forward loader, then fetched the tokens at that position and compared them with the scored July file. Both verified passages are license/header text.

| July test row (zero-based) | Language | Exact consecutive tokens | Training step (zero-based) |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4221 | C++ | 206 | 145,950 |
| 6200 | Python | 118 | 167,299 |

The third match was another license header (142 C++ tokens) in the training pool. Separately, at least three July files contain identifiable implementation code that predates August 2025, including Dear ImGui and urllib3. That date check establishes reuse of old code. The fraction of all July files seen during training remains unknown. [C++ training run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-main-step121638) · [Python training run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k) · [Training data order](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ad754c6d67555d6369a4a312ff7388e43cfd08c1/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/dataset.py) · [Official Stack v3 snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceCode/stack-v3-train)

An additional targeted scan of **1,609,826,304 training tokens** found zero exact 96-token matches that contained at least 16 identifier, operator or keyword positions outside strings and comments. This sample leaves most of the training stream unexamined. Removing all eight July files flagged by either the store or old-source checks leaves Mochi at **0.22560 C++ / 0.29255 Python**, versus **0.25346 / 0.33236** for Gemma on those same files.

### Newer official holdout candidate

The final Mochi run's nonzero training components point to the August Harrier store. The near-duplicate screen uses 13-token shingles with comments and whitespace removed and literals normalized. It excludes a candidate when at least 50% of its distinct shingles match one prior file and it contains at least 20 distinct shingles.

</details>

**Post-release cross-check.** We scanned the 22 November pilot files against the same 16.643B training tokens and found zero qualifying exact code matches. That small set is best used to check whether the October result transfers to files added after the checkpoint release.

### Post-release holdout pilot

The pilot retains **15 C++ files and 7 Python files from 22 repositories**, with one file per repository. Each corresponding pull request opened and merged November 18–22, after the November 17 Mochi release. The sample uses added files, pins each Git blob, and removes leading license headers from the scored text. [Mochi release](https://openathena.ai/blog/marin-mochi-pretraining-checkpoints/)

We screened for copied passages within the pilot, against the July benchmark, and against nearby files from the same repositories before release. A targeted scan of 201,326,592 Mochi training tokens found zero exact 96-token matches to the retained scored text. This small pilot provides examples for a fresher evaluation. 🤖 # Research

This issue requires two new model evaluations and a calibrated plot estimate; no result or overlapping PR is linked to #12173. The [preserved document-loss scorer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/snowball-document-losses-2026-09-16/experiments/evaluation/snowball_uncheatable_losses.py#L127-L181) already sums token loss and source bytes for BPB, and its [July manifest config](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/snowball-document-losses-2026-09-16/experiments/evaluation/configs/snowball_history_20260909/cooldown-42150.json) pins the requested dataset revision. Its [loader and tokenizer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/snowball-document-losses-2026-09-16/experiments/evaluation/snowball_uncheatable_losses.py#L339-L393) are Snowball specific; Levanter's aggregate BPB has separate known errors in [#10968](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10968).

# Proposed Fix

1. Check the pinned July manifest against Hugging Face revision `65889535d56aa38d448ce7e07b08e6e36c031545`; select the same 500 C++ and 500 Python documents for both models, recording IDs, text hashes, and byte counts. Keep evaluation data, checkpoint caches, and outputs in the execution region.
2. Validate a document scorer for the released Mochi step 393,491 and Gemma 4 31B base at the checkpoint revisions in this issue. Use each native tokenizer and 4,096-token windows; on a small diagnostic sample, check checkpoint loading, one count per predicted token, exclusion of auxiliary loss, and UTF-8 source-byte denominators. Adapt the preserved scorer only where the model loaders require it, then run both full evaluations on Iris and retain job links, configs, code revision, precision, and per-document exports.
3. For each model and language, compute BPB as `sum(token NLL) / (ln(2) × sum(source UTF-8 bytes))`; require 500 unique, finite records per language and report exclusions if any. Give C++ and Python equal weight for the model comparison. Compare Gemma's measured values with the published 0.25293 C++ and 0.33209 Python, including absolute and percentage differences.
4. Recover the DeepSeek V4 Pro Base and Kimi K2 Base reference coordinates from the [original plot](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972). Report Mochi's coordinate from the two-anchor mapping and from a fit that includes Gemma, with the numerical shift between them. State that Gemma's plot height is inferred and that mapping July code BPB to the plot's evaluation data adds uncertainty; use the older-to-July holdout errors already recorded in this issue as a sensitivity check.

If model support requires a code change, link its PR with `Part of #12173`; the final results should be recorded on this issue before it closes.

🤖 The 0.879 coordinate uses chart heights for Kimi K2 Base (in both fits) and Gemma 4 31B (in the three-anchor fit). Neither model is in the MAI report linked above or on Elie's chart. Where do those two heights come from?

[Figure 1 of the MAI report](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/Frontier-Pre-training-at-Microsoft-AI.pdf) gives code bits per byte (BPB) on MAI's codebase for six models: MAI-Base-1 0.2401, MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL 0.2446, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B 0.2400, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base 0.2370, Kimi K3 0.2264 and MAI-Base-2 0.2203. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base is the only outside base model, and the Kimi entry is the post-trained K3. Elie's chart converts these values with the MAI-Base-1/MAI-Base-2 line in step 3 below, which puts DeepSeek at 0.869 and Kimi K3 at 0.837. On the July C++/Python mean, Mochi (0.2577) sits 49.6% of the way from DeepSeek (0.2476) to Kimi K2 Base (0.2680, from #8824). The two-anchor 0.8788 therefore needs a Kimi K2 Base height of 0.889, which matches no Kimi point on the chart. If the Kimi K2 and Gemma heights were derived from DeepSeek and an assumed slope, the fit has one measured anchor. The 0.0103 chart-unit miss for held-out Gemma would then test that derivation. It would not test the mapping to OpenAI's evaluation.

We propose calibrating our code BPB directly against MAI's, using the four Figure 1 models with public weights. The report says only post-trained checkpoints of Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 and MiMo are available, so MAI scored the same weights we can download.

| Model | Active / total parameters (Figure 1) | MAI code BPB | July C++/Python mean BPB |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base | 49B / 1.6T | 0.2370 | 0.2476 (#8824) |
| Kimi K3, post-trained | 104B / 2.8T | 0.2264 | not scored |
| Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, post-trained | 95B / 2.4T | 0.2400 | not scored |
| MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL, post-trained | 42B / 1.02T | 0.2446 | not scored |

1. Score all four models and Mochi on the screened October split above (470 C++ and 490 Python files), with the scorer used here for Mochi and Gemma. Qwen3.8 and MiMo were released on August 8 and September 21, after the July files, so their training data may contain those files. All four were released before the October files were pushed, and the October screen already removed files that overlap Mochi's training data.
2. Fit MAI code BPB against our October BPB across the four models. Report the slope, the residuals and the leave-one-out errors.
3. Apply the fit to Mochi's October BPB, then map the result to the chart through MAI-Base-1 (0.2401 at 0.878) and MAI-Base-2 (0.2203 at 0.819): chart = 0.878 + 2.98 × (MAI BPB − 0.2401).

Each anchor in this chain is measured on both of the scales it connects. The chain still assumes a linear map from our code files to MAI's codebase, that post-trained checkpoints follow the same line as base models, and the MAI-Base-1/MAI-Base-2 line.

Expect large residuals. Across the 13 open base models in #8824, regressing the July C++/Python mean on Paloma's 100-language code subset leaves a residual standard deviation of 0.027 BPB (R² 0.54). If the MAI fit scatters that much, the chart coordinate carries about ±0.08 (0.027 × 2.98). The code set also matters. Mochi's BPB is 4.1% above DeepSeek's on the July C++/Python mean and 18.5% above on Paloma's code subset. At 1.79 chart units per BPB of gap from DeepSeek (2.98 × 0.60, the central slope on Elie's chart), that difference moves Mochi from 0.887 to 0.944.

@Calvin-Xu, we tested your loss-to-loss idea on newer UncheatableEval files. **A straight line captures a trend, with substantial scatter.** Using all 8 completed comparison models in one fit, final Mochi (step 393,491) lands at **0.243 ± 0.007 bits per byte on MAI code** and **0.888 ± 0.020 on Elie’s OpenAI log-perplexity axis**.

### What changed in the eval?

We switched from July after finding training code in 19 of its scored files. We screened the official October split against 16.643B tokens actually consumed during Mochi training. Of 1,000 candidate code files, we removed 21 with independently verified code matches and 19 more in the vendored/generated and near-duplicate screen. The audit covers a sample of Mochi’s training stream, so residual overlap is possible. [Pinned October dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-10/tree/87a300906c15c2433c5285035042dabdcbec0725)

Every model saw the same **470 C++ and 490 Python files**. We scored the observed tokens in 4,096-token windows, summed their loss per language, and divided by UTF-8 bytes. Giving the two languages equal weight yields **0.28696 bits per byte for Mochi**, directly measured on the public files.

### Does a straight line predict MAI code loss?

The plot pairs each model’s measured public-code loss with its published MAI code loss. To put both reports on the MAI-2 scale, we kept the MAI-1 report’s model-to-model differences and shifted its values by −0.0040 BPB, the change in their common MAI-Base-1 reference. Mochi’s public score falls inside the calibration range. [MAI-1 Figure 10](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf#page=24) · [MAI-2 Figure 1](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/Frontier-Pre-training-at-Microsoft-AI.pdf)

![The 8 measured model coordinates and fitted straight line relating public code loss to MAI code loss.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/mai-code-transfer-8.png)

The fit explains **69%** of the variation among these points. We also hid each entire model family, refitted on the others, and predicted the hidden scores. The resulting prediction error was **0.0068 BPB**. Each family contributes equally to the RMSE. That small set of families supports using a line for interpolation and leaves considerable uncertainty for a new family such as Mochi.

### How does Mochi score on the public files?

![Direct C++ and Python bits per byte for final Mochi and all completed comparison models.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/october-code-scores-8.png)

Additional direct measurements on the same files, averaged over the two languages, are Inkling 2 Mini **0.27889**, Inkling 2 Small **0.22817**, Reflection Beam 1.0 (instruction-tuned BF16) **0.24964** BPB. These checkpoints have no published MAI code score in the two reports, so the calibration still uses 8 models. For these checkpoints and MiMo, the scorer uses EOS before the first source token because the checkpoints have no declared BOS. [Comparison weights and per-language scores](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/additional-comparisons.json)

**Inkling 2 Mini versus Mochi.** Mini loses on C++ by 0.0158 BPB and wins on Python by 0.0320. With equal language weights, Mini averages 0.2789 to Mochi’s 0.2870, a 2.8% lower loss. Its advantage is 0.0081 BPB (95% paired file-bootstrap interval 0.0047–0.0113, resampling within each language). We screened overlap against Mochi’s training stream. Inkling’s training exposure to these files is unknown. [Paired results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/paired-extra-vs-mochi.json)

### Where does that put Mochi on Elie’s plot?

We mapped the predicted MAI code BPB through Elie’s MAI-1/MAI-2 calibration, using `0.878 + 2.98 × (MAI code BPB − 0.2401)`. Scaling the family-held-out RMSE by the same factor gives the transfer error quoted above. Uncertainty in the two-point OpenAI mapping is additional. OpenAI’s private evaluation remains unmeasured for Mochi. [Elie’s original plot](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972) · [Numerical results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/mai-code-transfer-8.json)

![Elie’s original layout with new October estimates for the public models and the orange Mochi point at 0.888.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/elie-style-october.png)

The blue OpenAI curve and red MAI anchors retain their published values. The teal, purple and orange markers all use our public-code loss measurements and the same MAI calibration. Kimi K3.1 Pro occupies the original Kimi proxy’s horizontal position. Its label names the released checkpoint we scored. GLM-5.3 uses its official `[gMASK]<sop>` start and lands at 0.877. [Vector figure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/elie-style-october.pdf)

### Where do the released Inkling models land?

The same line gives **0.843 ± 0.020** for Small and **0.882 ± 0.020** for Mini. Small lies just outside the range of measured calibration scores. Elie’s original Small point reads approximately **0.814**, a gap of **+0.029**. The checkpoint matters here. Thinking Machines reports 0.2030 BPB for pre-trained Small and 0.2080 for post-trained Small on its internal code. Applying the slope implied by Elie’s DeepSeek V4 Pro Base anchor and Small point to that difference puts the public checkpoint at about **0.823** on his scale. Our matched-version gap is **+0.020**. The hollow diamond below is our reconstruction. [Thinking Machines’ measurements](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) · [Placement calculations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/inkling-placement-8.json)

![Published and reconstructed Inkling Small coordinates alongside October estimates for Small, Mini, and Mochi.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/inkling-placement-8.png)

All eight open checkpoints in the two MAI comparisons are included. We have no scoring access to Microsoft’s MAI-L66, MAI-Base-1 or MAI-Base-2 checkpoints.

### Where do the other purple points land?

We scored the four remaining public checkpoints on the same 960 October files and reused the Inkling 2 Small measurement. GLM-5.3 uses its official `[gMASK]<sop>` start. Only the code tokens count toward loss. We held the eight-model calibration fixed. In the original comparison, Thinking Machines fine-tuned the released GLM, DeepSeek and Kimi weights on pretraining-formatted text to estimate base loss. Its Inkling point uses the pre-trained checkpoint. Our October scores use the released checkpoints directly. For Kimi, the measured release is **K3.1 Pro**, the model used to construct the purple point labeled “Kimi K3 base.” [Thinking Machines’ methods and original loss table](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/)

| Released checkpoint | C++ BPB | Python BPB | Mean BPB | Our chart estimate | Original purple point¹ | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [GLM-5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3/tree/ba32f8c19c8738e2c57c71798c601d477a7bf844) | 0.22056 | 0.32635 | 0.27345 | 0.877 | 0.873 | +0.004 |
| [GLM-5.3 Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/tree/46a050bec13002ad29ee795c16e61cf4fa3c4a9c) | 0.21865 | 0.31997 | 0.26931 | 0.874 | 0.867 | +0.007 |
| [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017/tree/08c8657f02291e11b6f6b63e0e16014f8e748518) | 0.20006 | 0.27887 | 0.23946 | 0.852 | 0.846 | +0.006 |
| [Kimi K3.1 Pro](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro/tree/d9e99b0792a5e93b78ea9bea62a68167e36ddd9e) | 0.17941 | 0.26522 | 0.22232 | 0.839 | 0.821 | +0.018 |
| [Inkling 2 Small](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Small/tree/885d78bfca61a7e9a498e33cfa7ad35850533b8c) | 0.19616 | 0.26018 | 0.22817 | 0.843 | 0.814 | +0.029 |

¹ Original coordinates were read from the purple square centers in Elie’s image. Difference is our estimate minus that point. The shared error scale is **±0.020** on the chart. The measured calibration range is 0.2286–0.3157 mean BPB. The following models require extrapolation: Kimi K3.1 Pro, Inkling 2 Small. The measured gaps combine checkpoint differences and transfer between code datasets, whose training overlap for these released models is unknown. [Results, pinned revisions, and original image coordinates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/purple-placement.json)

![Elie’s original five purple points and our estimates for the corresponding released checkpoints.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/purple-placement.png)

[All October measurements and checkpoint dates, including models outside the original chart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/october-model-timeline.json) · [Detailed plot of the 16 supported or near-range placements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/october-model-timeline.pdf)

### GLM-5.3 raw-code and template checks

GLM-5.3 scored **0.6917 BPB** under the common raw-code protocol. FP8 with eight-way tensor parallelism scored 0.8480 BPB. The official BF16 weights on sixteen GPUs scored 0.8174 BPB. The calibration anchors range from **0.2286 to 0.3157 BPB**. The timeline uses the official-start measurement in the table below.

We also scored all **960** files under five conditions on the same pinned FP8 release. Only source-code token losses enter the calculations. The complete chat conditions supply a short language-specific request to write a source file. One scores the code immediately after the opening thinking tag, the other as the answer after an empty thinking block.

| Text before the file | C++ BPB | Python BPB | Equal-language mean BPB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| EOS only | 0.8265 | 0.5160 | 0.6712 |
| [gMASK]<sop> | 0.2206 | 0.3263 | 0.2735 |
| Native start and default system instruction | 0.4842 | 0.4433 | 0.4638 |
| Official user and assistant prefix, open thinking block | 0.2412 | 0.3397 | 0.2905 |
| Official user and assistant prefix, closed thinking block | 0.4190 | 0.4108 | 0.4149 |

Changing only the initial token IDs from EOS to the official `[gMASK]<sop>` start reduced mean code loss by **59.3%** across the same 960 files. Individual loss fell for 469 of 470 C++ files and 348 of 490 Python files. The benchmark runner fell back to EOS because this tokenizer did not declare a BOS. The native start maps to **0.877** on our eight-model calibration. The corresponding square in Elie’s figure is **0.873**. Both the purple-point table and the main figure use this native-start estimate.

On file 4174, eight repeated scores with the same FP8 server and the same file spanned **1.915–5.260 BPB** with EOS and **0.221–0.226 BPB** with the native start. In the duplicate-prompt tests, the largest mean absolute token-logprob difference over a shared 256-token segment fell from **8.82** to **0.08 nats** on this FP8 configuration. The prefix explains a substantial part of the aggregate anomaly. The exact source of the residual inference variability is unresolved.

[Exact prefixes, paired file-bootstrap intervals and inference checks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/glm53-audit.json) · [Repeated-input diagnostics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/glm53-runtime-probes.json) · [Pinned official template](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3/blob/ba32f8c19c8738e2c57c71798c601d477a7bf844/chat_template.jinja)

With `--max-num-seqs 1` on eight GPUs, identical inputs produced identical file scores across all eight repeats for each of the five probe files, under both prefixes. File 4174 still scored **4.810 BPB** with EOS and **0.218 BPB** with the native start. Scoring one sequence at a time removed the repeat variability on these files while preserving the prefix effect. Shortening the prompts can still change shared-prefix logprobs in this mode. [Prompt-length and duplicate-input checks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/glm53-runtime-probes.json)
